title: How to Record a Referral Programme Discount for a New Customer's First Purchase
description: Recording a first-purchase discount given to a new customer referred by an existing loyalty member.
explanation: Referral discounts are a customer acquisition tool. Tracking them separately as contra-revenue allows measurement of the cost-per-acquisition through the referral channel.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Link the referral code entered at POS to the referring customer's profile in the loyalty system. This allows tracking of (1) how many new customers each referrer generates, (2) the acquisition cost (discount given), and (3) the lifetime value of referred customers vs. non-referred. VAT is on the net discounted price paid.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check that the referral discount is applied only once per new customer per referral code. Multiple referral discounts to the same customer number indicate a control weakness or abuse of the program. The referring customer may also receive a reward (credit or discount) — ensure that is separately recorded if applicable.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Referral program terms (discount rate, one-time use, referring customer tracking), POS referral code log, Sales Discounts (Referral) ledger, new customer registration record, and referral channel ROI analysis (acquisition cost vs. LTV).

title: How to Defer Revenue When Retail Customers Earn Loyalty Points at Purchase
description: Splitting a retail sale between recognized revenue and a deferred loyalty points liability under IFRS 15.
explanation: Under IFRS 15, loyalty points with standalone value are a separate performance obligation. The estimated redemption value is deferred until points are used or expire.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Integrate the loyalty platform with the ERP to automatically calculate and post the deferred points amount on each transaction. The standalone value of points equals the redemption value per point multiplied by the expected redemption rate (e.g., if 80% of points are redeemed, defer 80% of the points' face value). Reconcile the Loyalty Points Liability to the loyalty platform's outstanding points balance monthly.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The IFRS 15 allocation of transaction price requires a judgment on both the standalone value of points and the expected redemption rate. Auditors will test both assumptions against historical data. Under-deferring inflates current revenue; over-deferring deflates it — both are misstatements. Review the assumptions at least annually.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Loyalty program terms, standalone selling price calculation for points, historical redemption rate data, Loyalty Points Liability roll-forward, loyalty platform outstanding balance confirmation, and IFRS 15 performance obligation assessment.

title: How to Record Loyalty Points Redeemed Against a Retail Purchase
description: Converting the deferred loyalty points liability to earned revenue when a customer uses accumulated points.
explanation: Redemption converts the deferred points liability into earned revenue. The customer pays the balance in cash and the transaction is closed.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The POS loyalty integration deducts points at redemption and the ERP simultaneously debits Loyalty Points Liability and credits Sales Revenue. The total sale value (points + cash) equals the full retail price. For VAT: confirm with your tax advisor whether points constitute monetary consideration — typically the full retail price is the VAT base regardless of how it is paid.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors reconcile the Loyalty Points Liability roll-forward at year-end. Points redeemed should reduce the liability exactly by the redemption value. Any difference indicates unrecorded redemptions or posting errors. The revenue recognized on redemption must equal the value of points redeemed plus cash paid — not just the cash received.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Loyalty platform redemption report, Loyalty Points Liability roll-forward, Sales Revenue reconciliation including points-redeemed portion, VAT treatment memo for loyalty redemptions, and POS transaction record showing points deducted and cash received.

title: How to Recognize Loyalty Points Breakage Income from Expired or Unredeemed Points
description: Releasing the loyalty points liability to Other Income when points expire without being redeemed.
explanation: Points that pass their expiry date without redemption are an obligation that no longer exists. The liability is released to Other Income based on historical expiry rate assumptions.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Apply the IFRS 15 proportional breakage method — recognize breakage income in proportion to the pattern of points redemptions using the estimated non-redemption rate. This avoids a one-time large income hit at expiry and instead spreads the recognition proportionally. Run the breakage calculation monthly or quarterly based on the cohort issuance data.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: See gift-card-breakage-revenue for core breakage audit notes. For loyalty points, the additional consideration is whether the points expiry policy is consistently enforced — if the store routinely extends points expiry for customer retention, the breakage rate assumption is overstated. Auditors will check actual extension patterns against the breakage model.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Historical points redemption data by cohort, non-redemption rate calculation, IFRS 15 proportional breakage methodology memo, Loyalty Points Liability roll-forward, breakage income schedule, and extension policy document.

title: How to Record a Partial Gift Card Redemption with a Cash Top-Up
description: Recognizing revenue when a customer partially uses a gift card and pays the remaining balance in cash.
explanation: The gift card value offsets part of the sale. The remainder is paid in cash. Only the portion actually used converts to revenue — the remaining balance stays as a liability.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The Gift Card Liability sub-ledger must accurately track each card's remaining balance after every partial redemption. The POS scan should show the customer their remaining balance after the transaction. Multiple partial redemptions are common — each must update the sub-ledger correctly. Full revenue and VAT are recognized on the total sale value (gift card + cash), not just the cash portion.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors spot-check the Gift Card Liability sub-ledger by tracing individual card transactions from issuance through all partial redemptions to the current remaining balance. Any discrepancy in a card's history indicates a system error or potential manipulation. The total sub-ledger should reconcile exactly to the GL Gift Card Liability balance.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Gift card transaction history (issuance, each redemption with date and amount, remaining balance), POS transaction records for each partial redemption, Gift Card Liability sub-ledger reconciliation, and year-end breakage analysis for cards nearing expiry.

title: How to Issue Store Credit to a Customer and Record the Deferred Liability
description: Creating a store credit balance for a customer instead of a cash refund, reversing the original sale.
explanation: A store credit is a liability — the store owes the customer merchandise or services. Revenue is reversed and the credit balance is held until the customer spends it.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Issue store credit via a unique credit note number linked to the customer's account. The Store Credit Liability sub-ledger tracks each customer's balance. When credit is redeemed for a new purchase, it converts to revenue. Set an expiry date for store credits (if policy allows) and track aging — credits outstanding more than 12 months may qualify for breakage income recognition.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: See ret-return-store-credit-issued for the return-specific audit considerations. For standalone store credit issuances (e.g., as a promotion), the liability must be recognized until redeemed or expired. Auditors will reconcile the Store Credit Liability sub-ledger to the GL balance and test for aged balances that should be released to breakage income.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Store credit note (amount, customer, date, expiry if applicable), Store Credit Liability sub-ledger, redemption tracking, aging analysis, breakage income recognition schedule, and policy document governing credit expiry.

title: How to Record a Store Credit Redemption on a Customer Purchase
description: Converting a store credit balance to earned revenue and recognizing COGS when a customer redeems their credit.
explanation: When credit is redeemed, the liability converts to earned revenue and COGS is recognized. No cash changes hands — the transaction is settled through the credit balance.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: At credit redemption, the POS or ERP must simultaneously: debit the Store Credit Liability, credit Sales Revenue and VAT, and post the COGS entry. The customer's store credit balance updates to zero (or the remaining balance for partial redemptions). The total sale value for VAT purposes is the full retail price of the goods received, even though payment was entirely non-cash.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that revenue recognized on credit redemption equals the retail price of goods sold — not the amount of credit used. If the credit balance covers more than the purchase price, the excess credit should remain in the liability, not be released to revenue. COGS must be recognized on the full value of goods regardless of payment method.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: POS redemption transaction, Store Credit Liability updated sub-ledger balance, Sales Revenue and VAT output entries, COGS entry, and physical goods transfer confirmation.

title: How to Record an Inventory Purchase Paid Immediately in Cash
description: Recording a stock purchase from a supplier with immediate cash payment, creating an inventory asset.
explanation: Inventory purchased for cash is immediately an asset at cost. It remains on the balance sheet until sold, when it transfers to Cost of Goods Sold.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Always create a purchase order before paying cash to a supplier — this ensures a three-way match (PO, receiving note, payment) is possible even for cash transactions. Record the inventory at net cost (excluding VAT, which is a separate recoverable asset). For cash purchases from informal vendors without VAT invoices, the input tax cannot be recovered — factor this into sourcing decisions.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Cash inventory purchases are higher-risk than credit purchases because there is no payable to match against. Auditors will require a delivery note or receipt to confirm goods were received. Cash payments to unknown or unregistered suppliers without adequate documentation will be disallowed by ISTD as a deductible expense.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Purchase order, supplier delivery note or receipt, cash payment record (petty cash voucher or bank transfer), inventory receiving log, three-way match confirmation, and supplier registration status.

title: How to Record an Inventory Purchase on 30-Day Credit Terms Including Recoverable VAT
description: Recording a stock delivery on credit terms, separating the net inventory cost from the recoverable VAT input.
explanation: Inventory is an asset the moment it arrives, regardless of when the supplier is paid. VAT on the purchase is a separate recoverable asset — not part of inventory cost.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The ERP should automatically split the supplier invoice into net inventory cost and VAT Input Tax based on the tax code applied. Never include VAT in the inventory account — it is a separate recoverable asset that flows into the monthly VAT return to offset output VAT. Maintain a supplier payables sub-ledger with invoice-level detail for payment scheduling.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: VAT input tax claims require a valid VAT invoice showing the supplier's TRN. Purchases from unregistered suppliers generate no recoverable VAT. Auditors check that TRNs on supplier invoices are valid before accepting input tax claims. Year-end cut-off testing ensures goods received before period-end are in both inventory and payables.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Supplier VAT invoice (with TRN, net amount, VAT, total), delivery note, purchase order, three-way match record, VAT Input Tax register, AP sub-ledger entry, and payment schedule.

title: How to Record a Quantity Discrepancy Claim When a Supplier Delivers Fewer Units Than Invoiced
description: Raising a debit note and reducing both inventory and payables when the supplier's delivery is short.
explanation: A quantity discrepancy is resolved by reducing both inventory and the payable by the value of the missing goods. A formal debit note is sent to the supplier.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Use a Goods Receipt / Invoice Receipt (GR/IR) process in the ERP: receive goods at the actual delivered quantity, then match the supplier invoice. The system flags the discrepancy. Issue a formal debit note to the supplier for the short-delivered units. Do not pay the full invoice until the discrepancy is resolved or a credit note is received from the supplier.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test GR/IR clearing accounts for unresolved discrepancies. Persistent short-delivery discrepancies with the same supplier may indicate a systemic supplier reliability issue or a receiving process failure. Discrepancies above a materiality threshold should be investigated before payment and resolved with a formal supplier credit note.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Goods received note (actual quantity received), supplier invoice (invoiced quantity), discrepancy report, formal debit note sent to supplier, supplier credit note received, and GR/IR clearing account reconciliation.

title: How to Capitalize Freight-In Charges into the Cost of Received Inventory
description: Adding inbound freight costs to the inventory cost under IAS 2 so that COGS reflects the full landed cost.
explanation: Under IAS 2, all costs to bring inventory to its present location must be included in its cost. Freight-in is capitalized into inventory, increasing COGS when items are sold.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Use a landed cost module in the ERP to distribute freight (and other inbound costs like insurance, customs, clearing) across the items in each shipment. Common allocation methods: by value (proportional to item cost), by weight, or by volume. The allocated freight per unit becomes part of the item's unit cost in the ERP and flows into COGS at point of sale.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Expensing freight-in as a period cost (rather than capitalizing it into inventory) understates inventory value and overstates current-period COGS — a misstatement under IAS 2. Auditors test whether the landed cost methodology is consistently applied. For large shipments, the freight allocation is material and may be tested in detail.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Freight invoice or carrier's bill of lading, landed cost allocation calculation (allocation method and per-item amount), inventory receiving record showing updated unit cost, and ERP landed cost module configuration.

title: How to Record Consignment Inventory Shipped to a Dealer While Retaining Ownership
description: Transferring goods to a dealer's showroom on consignment — recorded as an asset reclassification, not a sale.
explanation: Consignment outbound is a transfer between two asset accounts — not a sale. The goods remain the store's property until the dealer makes a sale.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: See consignment-inventory-outbound-shipment for full ERP notes. Confirm the consignment agreement is signed before any goods leave the warehouse. Use location tracking in the ERP to distinguish home stock from consignment stock. Monthly, request a stock-on-hand report from each dealer and reconcile to the Inventory on Consignment sub-ledger.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: See consignment-inventory-outbound-shipment for full audit notes. Highlight: at year-end, all consignment stock held at dealers must be included in the consignor's inventory balance — this stock is NOT the dealer's asset and should not appear in the dealer's inventory. Obtain signed dealer confirmations at year-end.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Consignment agreement, outbound delivery note, Inventory on Consignment sub-ledger by dealer, monthly dealer stock reports, year-end dealer confirmation letters, and reconciliation of consignment stock to the GL.

title: How to Record an Inter-Store Inventory Transfer Between Branches
description: Moving stock from one store or warehouse to a branch with low inventory — an internal transfer with no P&L impact.
explanation: Inter-store transfers are internal movements with no P&L impact. Total inventory value is unchanged — it is reclassified between locations.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Process inter-store transfers via a formal transfer order in the ERP or WMS — never move stock informally without a system record. The transfer requires: a dispatch record from Branch A, a receiving record at Branch B, and a transfer order linking both. Until Branch B confirms receipt, the stock should be in an 'In-Transit' account. Investigate any transfers that remain in-transit beyond 48 hours.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors trace inter-store transfers to verify they are genuine stock movements and not fictitious entries used to manipulate individual store performance metrics. A high volume of transfers from a low-performing store to a high-performing store near period-end may indicate stock manipulation to affect bonuses or KPIs.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Transfer order (items, quantities, transferring store, receiving store), dispatch note from Branch A (signed), receiving note from Branch B (signed), in-transit account reconciliation, and monthly inter-store transfer activity report.

title: How to Record a Drop-Shipment Where the Supplier Ships Directly to the Customer
description: Recording a sale where no inventory is held — the supplier ships directly to the customer and revenue and COGS are recognized simultaneously.
explanation: In dropshipping, no inventory asset is ever created. Revenue and COGS are recognized simultaneously at the time of the customer order.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: In a dropship model, the ERP must link the customer sales order to a purchase order raised against the drop-ship supplier. When the supplier confirms dispatch, both the revenue (customer order) and the COGS/payable (supplier PO) are posted simultaneously. No inventory account is touched. Track dropship orders separately to measure the dropship channel margin vs. direct inventory margin.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The principal vs. agent analysis is critical in dropshipping — if the store genuinely controls the goods and bears inventory risk (even briefly), it is the principal and gross revenue is correct. If the store is merely facilitating a transaction without bearing risk, it may be an agent (commission revenue only). Auditors will review the dropship agreement to determine the correct presentation.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Customer order confirmation, supplier drop-ship purchase order, supplier dispatch confirmation, delivery confirmation to customer, sales invoice to customer, supplier invoice received, IFRS 15 principal vs. agent assessment, and dropship channel margin report.

title: How to Record an Advance Payment to a Supplier for Future Seasonal Stock
description: Paying a supplier in advance for a large seasonal order, recording the payment as a current asset.
explanation: Supplier advances are current assets — not expenses. They convert to inventory when the goods are delivered and the supplier's invoice is received.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Maintain an Advances to Suppliers sub-ledger per supplier showing the amount paid, expected delivery date, and status. As each delivery is received and invoiced, offset the advance against the inventory received. At year-end, any advance outstanding where delivery has not occurred (or is past the expected date) should be reviewed for recoverability — a supplier that fails to deliver may require an impairment of the advance.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Supplier advances outstanding at year-end are tested for recoverability. Auditors will confirm the delivery is still expected and request supplier confirmation. Advances to suppliers who are in financial difficulty or who have stopped communicating must be impaired or written off. Large advances to single suppliers without purchase orders or formal agreements are a control weakness.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Purchase order for the anticipated delivery, bank payment confirmation, Advances to Suppliers sub-ledger, expected delivery date documentation, supplier correspondence confirming the order, and impairment assessment for any overdue advances.

title: How to Settle a Supplier Advance Against Inventory Received on Delivery
description: Converting the supplier advance to inventory when the pre-paid goods are received.
explanation: When the goods arrive, the advance converts to inventory. If the actual invoice differs from the advance amount, cash or a payable balances the difference.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Process the goods receipt in the ERP using the received quantities and the supplier invoice amount. If the advance exactly matches the invoice, the settlement is a clean reclassification from Advances to Suppliers to Merchandise Inventory. If there is a difference (more or less delivered than advanced), the difference is either (a) an additional payable to the supplier or (b) a refund from the supplier.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that the inventory received matches the delivery note and that the advance sub-ledger is cleared. Any advance balance remaining after delivery (and not explained by a partial delivery or dispute) must be investigated. Advances for goods that were never delivered require immediate write-off or refund pursuit.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Supplier invoice matching the advance amount, goods received note confirming delivery, ERP advance clearance entry, difference reconciliation (if advance ≠ invoice), and Advances to Suppliers sub-ledger showing zero balance after settlement.

title: How to Calculate and Record COGS Under a Periodic Inventory System
description: Calculating cost of goods sold at period-end using the periodic method: opening inventory plus purchases minus closing inventory.
explanation: Under the periodic system, COGS = Opening Inventory + Purchases - Closing Inventory. The closing inventory figure comes from the physical count. COGS is calculated and recorded as one entry at period-end.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The periodic system is simpler but provides less real-time inventory control than perpetual. It requires a physical count at each period-end to determine closing inventory. COGS is calculated as a residual (opening + purchases − closing) rather than tracked per transaction. Most modern retail ERP systems use perpetual — periodic is more common in smaller operations without barcode/POS integration.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The closing inventory count is the foundation of the COGS calculation in the periodic system — any error in the count directly flows to COGS. Auditors will observe or independently verify the physical count. The COGS figure cannot be independently validated at the transaction level (unlike perpetual), making the count even more critical.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Opening inventory balance, all purchase invoices for the period, physical closing count sheets (signed and dated), COGS calculation (opening + purchases − closing = COGS), and auditor count observation record.

title: How to Record COGS Per Sale Under a Perpetual Inventory System
description: Recognizing cost of goods sold at the point of each individual sale in a perpetual inventory system.
explanation: In a perpetual system, COGS is recognized on every sale transaction. The inventory balance is updated in real-time.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: In a perpetual system with POS/barcode integration, the COGS entry is automatic — the POS scan triggers the inventory deduction and COGS recognition in the ERP. The cost used is based on the cost method elected (FIFO, AVCO/WAC, or specific identification). Ensure the cost method is applied consistently — changing methods requires disclosure and comparative restatement.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: In a perpetual system, the COGS per transaction is testable — auditors can trace individual sales to the specific cost layer consumed (FIFO lot, WAC rate). Discrepancies between the perpetual COGS and the physical count-based COGS (using the periodic method as a check) indicate either unrecorded shrinkage or system errors.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: POS transaction report with COGS per item, cost method policy document (FIFO or WAC), inventory movement ledger, periodic physical count as a cross-check, COGS reconciliation (perpetual total vs. periodic calculation), and year-end shrinkage adjustment.

title: How to Write Down Inventory to Net Realizable Value Under IAS 2
description: Reducing the carrying value of inventory when NRV falls below cost due to price drops or obsolescence.
explanation: Under IAS 2, inventory must be reported at the lower of cost or NRV. This is especially relevant for fashion, electronics, and perishable goods where prices can drop quickly.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Run a monthly NRV review comparing the current expected selling price (less selling costs) to the inventory unit cost for each active SKU. Where NRV < cost, calculate the write-down per unit × quantity on hand and post to Inventory Write-Down Expense. Under IFRS, NRV write-downs are reversible if market prices recover (up to original cost) — track write-down history per SKU for reversal assessment.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: NRV assessments are highly judgmental — auditors will challenge the expected selling price assumptions, especially for items where the planned selling price has been reduced post-period-end. Items sold at a loss after year-end are evidence that NRV was below cost at year-end, requiring a write-down that management may have avoided. The write-down must capture all items where NRV < cost, not just selected SKUs.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: NRV calculation per SKU (expected selling price minus selling costs, compared to unit cost), pricing evidence (POS data, markdown schedules, competitor prices), management approval for write-down, subsequent sale data confirming NRV estimates, and IFRS IAS 2 NRV assessment memo.

title: How to Record Inventory Damage and an Insurance Claim Receivable
description: Recording stock destroyed by flooding or fire and the corresponding insurance claim at estimated recoverable value.
explanation: The inventory loss and insurance recovery are recorded separately. The loss is the full inventory value; the claim is what the insurer agrees to pay. Any shortfall is a net loss.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The Insurance Claim Receivable is recognized only when it is virtually certain the insurer will pay — a submitted claim does not meet this threshold until accepted. Use a probability-weighted estimate of the recovery as the receivable amount. Monitor the claim status and update the receivable if the insurer revises its assessment. The net loss (inventory cost minus insurance recovery) is the true economic impact.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors require evidence that the damage actually occurred (incident report, photographs, third-party damage assessment) and that the insurance policy covers the specific event. The insurance claim receivable is tested for recoverability — if the insurer disputes the claim, it may need to be impaired. ISTD may require documentation to allow the inventory loss as a tax deduction.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Incident report (date, cause, photos of damage), insurance policy confirming coverage, insurance claim submission, insurer's provisional acceptance or assessment, inventory loss calculation at cost, net loss (cost minus claim), and ISTD documentation for tax deduction.

title: How to Record a Cycle Count Overage When Physical Stock Exceeds the System Balance
description: Adjusting inventory upward when a physical count finds more units than the perpetual system shows.
explanation: An overage means the system underestimated stock — perhaps due to a missed receiving entry. The inventory is adjusted upward and the gain is recognized as Other Income.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Before posting an overage, investigate the cause — most overages are due to receiving entries that were missed in the system (goods received but not processed). If a receiving entry is found, post the missing receipt to both inventory and payables rather than recording it as Other Income. Only truly unexplained overages (after investigation) should go to Other Income.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Overages credited to Other Income without investigation are a red flag — they may represent unrecorded purchases (underreporting of payables) or other recording errors. Auditors expect management to investigate the cause of material overages before recognizing income. Genuine unexplained overages are rare in well-controlled perpetual systems.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Cycle count sheet (signed), investigation notes confirming whether a missing receiving entry was found, correcting entry if a receiving entry was the cause (inventory + payable, not Other Income), Inventory Overage Income ledger for genuine unexplained surpluses, and monthly overage/shortage trend analysis.

title: How to Write Off Completely Unsellable Dead Stock Against the Allowance Account
description: Removing fully obsolete inventory from the books by drawing against the previously established allowance account.
explanation: When dead stock is physically disposed of, both the inventory and any previously established allowance are removed. If no provision exists, the full cost is expensed directly.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The write-off draws against the Allowance for Obsolescence rather than creating a new expense — the cost was already recognized when the provision was established. If the write-off amount exceeds the allowance balance, the excess is expensed to Inventory Obsolescence Expense directly. After the write-off, the physical goods must be disposed of — do not leave zero-value items in the warehouse without a disposal record.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: See inventory-obsolescence-actual-disposal for full audit notes. The additional consideration for dead stock is the disposal method — liquidation (sold below cost), donation, or destruction. Each method has different tax and VAT implications. Auditors require physical disposal evidence regardless of whether the write-off was pre-provisioned or expensed directly.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Disposal authorization, disposal evidence (liquidation invoice, donation receipt, or destruction certificate), write-off calculation (against allowance or direct expense), post-disposal confirmation items are no longer in the warehouse, and tax/VAT treatment memo for the disposal method used.

title: How to Release Monthly Store Rent Expense from a Prepaid Annual Payment
description: Recognizing one month of store rent from a prepaid annual payment, matching the cost to the trading period.
explanation: Common in Jordan where landlords require 12 months upfront. The prepaid balance is released at JOD 2,500/month to match the occupancy cost to each trading period.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Set up a 12-month auto-amortization schedule in the ERP releasing JOD 2,500 on the first of each month. Under IFRS 16, leases longer than 12 months that are not short-term may require recognition of a right-of-use asset and lease liability — assess whether your lease qualifies for the short-term exemption. Withholding tax on rent to individual landlords (5%) must be tracked separately.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check the Prepaid Rent balance against the number of months remaining in the lease — the balance should equal remaining months × monthly rent. Any balance above this indicates a missed amortization entry. IFRS 16 compliance is also tested for longer leases — failure to recognize a right-of-use asset when required understates both assets and liabilities.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement, bank payment confirmation, prepaid amortization schedule, IFRS 16 assessment memo (short-term lease exemption analysis), withholding tax records, and monthly GL release confirmation.

title: How to Accrue Monthly Store Utility Costs Before the Bills Arrive
description: Estimating and recording electricity and water costs for the month under the accrual basis.
explanation: Under the accrual basis, utilities consumed during the month must be recognized even if the bill arrives in the following month.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Use prior months' bills to estimate the current month's accrual. Set up a reversing auto-journal on the first of the following month so that when the actual bill arrives, the net P&L effect is just the difference between estimate and actual. Track utilities as a percentage of revenue monthly — peak energy use periods (Ramadan, summer) require higher accruals.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Accruals that are never reversed when the actual bill arrives create double-counting. Auditors check the Accrued Liabilities balance at year-end to confirm it corresponds to genuine outstanding invoices. An accrual for the December utility bill that never gets reversed in January indicates a misstatement of prior-year expenses.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Prior-month utility bills (for accrual basis), current-month meter reading if available, accrual calculation, reversing entry when actual bill is received, year-end Accrued Liabilities analysis, and utility cost per sqm trend.

title: How to Record Store Cleaning and Maintenance Service Costs
description: Expensing monthly cleaning service and routine maintenance costs as operating expenses.
explanation: Routine cleaning and maintenance keep the store presentable and functional. These are operating expenses recognized in the month the service is provided.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: For monthly service contracts, accrue if the invoice arrives after period-close. Separate routine cleaning (expense) from any significant maintenance that enhances or extends the store's useful life (which may require capitalization). Track cleaning costs per sqm of store space as a benchmarking metric.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Significant maintenance invoices are tested for the repair vs. capital improvement distinction. Painting, replacing broken tiles, or fixing plumbing are expenses. Installing a new shopfront or expanding the store layout may qualify as a leasehold improvement (capitalizable). Auditors will review large maintenance invoices to confirm appropriate treatment.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Service provider invoice with work description, service agreement (for recurring contracts), Cleaning & Maintenance Expense ledger, and capital vs. expense assessment for significant maintenance work.

title: How to Record Monthly Store Security System and CCTV Monitoring Fees
description: Expensing the monthly monitoring subscription for the alarm system and CCTV as a loss prevention cost.
explanation: Security monitoring is a necessary overhead for any physical retail store — it protects against theft and reduces shrinkage losses.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Security monitoring subscriptions are monthly operating expenses. The security system hardware itself (cameras, alarm panels) is a fixed asset capitalized and depreciated. Separate the hardware (capital) from the monitoring service (expense). Track security costs relative to shrinkage to assess the ROI of the security investment.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors may ask for evidence that the security system is operational and actively monitored — particularly if significant shrinkage losses are claimed without a credible deterrence system in place. Security costs are a deductible business expense but must relate to the business premises (not personal property protection).
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Security service agreement (provider, coverage, monthly fee), payment records, Security & Loss Prevention Expense ledger, hardware capitalization record (separate from monitoring), and loss prevention effectiveness report (shrinkage rate trend).

title: How to Record Shopping Bag and Packaging Material Costs as a Selling Expense
description: Expensing branded shopping bags, tissue paper, and boxes as a cost of presenting purchases to customers.
explanation: Packaging materials are a selling cost expensed when purchased or consumed. Premium packaging for luxury retail is a meaningful cost tracked for margin analysis.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: For high-volume packaged goods, maintain a packaging supplies inventory account and expense as consumed. For lower volumes, expense on purchase. Track packaging cost per transaction as a unit economics metric. Consider Jordan's environmental levies on single-use plastic bags — if applicable, the levy is an additional cost to the retailer.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Packaging materials should be purchased for business use. Auditors verify that quantities are reasonable relative to transaction volumes. Bulk packaging purchases significantly in excess of sales volume may indicate stock is being used for non-business purposes.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Packaging supplier invoice, Store Supplies & Packaging Expense ledger, packaging cost per transaction analysis, and supplies inventory count (if bulk purchased).

title: How to Record Store Signage and Visual Merchandising Display Costs
description: Expensing seasonal promotional signage and window display materials as marketing costs.
explanation: In-store signage and window displays are marketing costs expensed in the period they are used. Permanent signage above the capitalization threshold would be capitalized as a leasehold improvement.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Seasonal display materials (posters, banners, printed signs) are period marketing expenses. Permanent branded signage (illuminated fascia, carved logo, LED displays) that is attached to the building is a leasehold improvement — capitalize if above the threshold. Track display material costs by season/campaign to assess visual merchandising ROI.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The expense vs. capitalize decision on signage depends on permanence and cost. Auditors test large signage invoices to confirm the correct treatment. Permanent illuminated external signage incorrectly expensed as printing costs understates fixed assets and understates depreciation in future periods.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Printing or fabrication invoice with item description, installation records (for permanent signage), Marketing & Visual Merchandising Expense ledger, campaign effectiveness report, and capitalization assessment for permanent signage.

title: How to Record an Annual In-Store Music Copyright License Fee as a Prepaid Asset
description: Paying the annual music copyright license for playing background music in the retail store, amortized monthly.
explanation: Playing music commercially requires a license. The annual fee is a prepaid asset amortized monthly at JOD 50.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Set up a 12-month amortization schedule for the music license. Below-threshold amounts may be expensed immediately for simplicity. Maintain the license certificate in the compliance file — operating without a valid music license exposes the store to copyright infringement claims. Streaming services (Spotify, Apple Music) for commercial use require a commercial license, not a personal subscription.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Music licenses are routine and low-risk. Auditors check that the license is current and that the amortization is correctly set up. If a personal streaming subscription is being used commercially and claimed as a business expense, this is both a compliance issue (no commercial license) and potentially a personal expense disallowance.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Music license certificate (provider, period covered, venues included), payment receipt, prepaid amortization schedule, and commercial use confirmation.

title: How to Record ATM and Cash Handling Service Fees Paid to the Bank
description: Expensing cash counting, coin rolling, and change provision fees paid to the bank as an operating cost.
explanation: High-volume cash retailers pay banks to count and process cash. This is an operating expense discovered on the bank statement during reconciliation.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Cash handling fees are typically auto-debited by the bank and identified during the monthly bank reconciliation. Post to Bank & Cash Handling Expense when reconciling. Track as part of the total cost of cash vs. card payment processing — high cash-handling fees may make a push toward card payments economically attractive.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Cash handling fees are straightforward and low-risk. Auditors check that they appear in the bank reconciliation and are correctly categorized. Unusual or unexpectedly large fees should be queried with the bank.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Bank statement showing the fee, bank service agreement confirming the fee schedule, bank reconciliation, and Bank & Cash Handling Expense ledger.

title: How to Record Monthly Gross Payroll for Sales Floor Staff Including Cashiers and Supervisors
description: Recording the gross wage expense for all store floor staff in the month they are earned.
explanation: Gross payroll is recognized as an expense in the month earned. The net amount is paid after deducting SSC employee share and income tax withholding.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Run the payroll calculation in the payroll system before posting to the ERP. The ERP receives: gross wages to Wages Expense, SSC employee deduction reducing Wages Payable, income tax withholding reducing Wages Payable, and net pay as a payable to employees. Reconcile headcount on payroll to the HR system — ghost employees are a classic retail fraud risk.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors reconcile the payroll to employment contracts and attendance records. POS login records can be used to corroborate that staff on payroll actually worked during the period. SSC filings must match payroll totals — any discrepancy triggers an SSC audit. The payroll is also cross-referenced to the EOSB provision to confirm all employees are included.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Payroll register (employee name, role, gross salary, deductions, net pay), employment contracts, attendance records, SSC registration for all employees, bank transfer records for net salary payments, and EOSB provision reconciliation to payroll headcount.

title: How to Record Commission-Based Staff Payouts for Sales Target Achievement
description: Paying monthly sales commissions to store staff based on individual or team sales targets achieved.
explanation: Commissions are earned when the sale occurs and matched to that period. They are a variable labour cost that scales with revenue.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Pull the individual sales report from the POS system to calculate each staff member's commissions. Commissions must be included in the SSC base and, where applicable, income tax withholding — they are part of total remuneration, not separate from it. Accrue commissions in the period the sales occur; pay in the following month with the regular payroll.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Commission schemes must be documented in employment contracts or a signed commission plan. Unauthorized commission payments or payments above the contracted rate are an audit finding. SSC authorities will verify that commissions are included in the insurable salary base — a common omission.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Commission plan document, POS individual sales report for the period, commission calculation per employee, SSC calculation including commissions, payroll record showing commissions paid, and signed commission plan acknowledgment from each employee.

title: How to Record Wages for Part-Time or Seasonal Retail Staff Hired for Peak Periods
description: Expensing wages for temporary staff hired for Ramadan, Eid, or holiday shopping peaks.
explanation: Seasonal hiring is common in retail. These wages are expensed in the period worked. Short-duration staff typically do not accumulate EOSB under Jordanian law.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Even for short-term staff, SSC registration is required if employment lasts more than one month. Keep employment contracts for seasonal staff documenting the fixed term to confirm no ongoing EOSB obligation. Track the total seasonal labor cost as a percentage of peak-period revenue — the benchmark helps plan future season staffing.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: SSC compliance for seasonal staff is frequently audited. Staff working more than the contractual threshold may be entitled to EOSB — review Jordan's labor law thresholds carefully. Paying seasonal wages in cash without proper records creates a disallowance risk with ISTD.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Fixed-term employment contracts, attendance records, payroll register, SSC registration (if required), bank or cash payment records, and EOSB entitlement assessment per labor law.

title: How to Record the Employer SSC Contribution for Retail Staff in Jordan
description: Recording the employer's mandatory 14.25% Social Security contribution for all enrolled retail employees.
explanation: The employer's SSC contribution is a mandatory labour cost in Jordan, recognized in the same period as the related wages expense.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The employer SSC (14.25%) is separate from the employee contribution (7.5%) which is deducted from gross pay. Both are remitted together to the SSC by the 15th of the following month. The employer SSC is an additional employment cost — it increases the fully-loaded cost of each employee beyond their gross salary. Include it in labor cost-per-transaction analysis.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: SSC auditors cross-reference submitted payrolls to ISTD records and can audit up to 5 prior years. All employees (including seasonal, part-time, and probationary) must be enrolled from their first day. SSC penalties for late registration or under-reporting are significant. Commissions and overtime must be included in the SSC base.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Monthly SSC calculation (per employee: insurable salary, employer contribution, employee deduction), SSC Form 4 monthly submission, SSC payment receipt by the 15th, and employee SSC registration certificates.

title: How to Accrue the Monthly EOSB Provision for Permanent Retail Staff in Jordan
description: Building the statutory end-of-service gratuity liability each month for all permanent retail employees.
explanation: Jordanian labour law requires a gratuity payment when an employee resigns or is terminated. Monthly provisioning avoids a large unexpected cost.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Calculate monthly as: (current gross monthly salary ÷ 12) × months of service for each employee. Update when salaries change — the provision must reflect the current salary (not the hire salary). Maintain a per-employee EOSB sub-ledger so the total provision balance reconciles to the sum of individual entitlements. Non-current for long-serving employees.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors independently recalculate a sample of EOSB provisions to verify accuracy. The most common error is using historical salary rates instead of current rates. All permanent employees (not just full-time) must be included. EOSB for part-time staff is proportional to hours worked if they meet the qualifying period under Jordan's Labor Law.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: EOSB calculation schedule per employee (start date, current salary, service months, provision amount), payroll records confirming current salary, Provision for EOSB reconciliation (opening + accruals − payouts = closing), and Labor Law compliance note.

title: How to Record Staff Uniform Purchases for Retail Store Employees
description: Expensing branded polo shirts, aprons, and name badges for all store staff.
explanation: Uniforms are expensed in the period purchased. They are a staff welfare and brand presentation cost.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Expense uniform purchases in the period of purchase if below the capitalization threshold. Significant branded uniform investments (e.g., full franchise launch) may warrant capitalization if the useful life exceeds the accounting period. Obtain receipts from employees acknowledging receipt of uniforms — this documents that the expense is genuine and protects against disputes about personal use.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Only branded, role-specific uniforms that cannot reasonably be worn outside of work are fully deductible. Casual clothing (non-branded shirts, generic trousers) is disallowed by ISTD. Retain the uniform design spec and photographs to confirm branding. Uniforms provided to owners or managers that double as personal wardrobe items are a disallowance risk.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Uniform supplier invoice with item description, uniform design spec or photograph confirming branding, employee acknowledgment of receipt, Staff Uniforms Expense ledger, and tax deductibility assessment.

title: How to Record Staff Training and Development Costs as an Operating Expense
description: Expensing customer service, sales technique, and product knowledge training for store staff.
explanation: Training is an operating expense. It improves staff capability but cannot be capitalized as an asset since the company does not own the knowledge.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Training costs are period expenses under IAS 38 — the trained knowledge resides in the employee, not the company. Expenses include: external trainer fees, course materials, venue hire, and travel to training locations. Internal trainer salaries already on payroll are not separately expensed (they are in Wages Expense). Track training cost per employee trained as an HR metric.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Training costs that primarily benefit the employee personally (professional qualification that transfers to any employer) may be treated as a taxable employment benefit. Auditors distinguish between role-specific training (product knowledge, POS systems) which is a business cost, and transferable professional qualifications (accounting certifications, MBA courses) which may be personal benefits.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Training provider invoice, course description confirming business relevance, attendee list, Staff Training & Development Expense ledger, and benefit assessment for any transferable qualifications.

title: How to Capitalize Store Fit-Out and Leasehold Improvement Costs
description: Recording the cost of fitting out a new store — flooring, shelving, and lighting — as a capitalized fixed asset.
explanation: Permanent improvements to a rented store are capitalized as a fixed asset, depreciated over the shorter of the lease term or useful life — typically 5–10 years.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Accumulate all fit-out costs in a capital project account during the fit-out period — do not depreciate until the store opens and the asset is available for use. Costs to include: contractor fees for structural work, electrical, plumbing, air conditioning, shelving, and lighting installation. Exclude: loose furniture below the capitalization threshold, small decorative items, and staff training costs for the new store opening.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Fit-out costs are a significant capital expenditure and receive detailed audit scrutiny. Auditors test individual invoices to confirm they are genuine improvements (not repairs, not personal items). The useful life assumption must be justified — a fit-out for a 5-year lease that the store expects to renew indefinitely should still be depreciated over 5 years unless the renewal is contractually certain.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Architect or design brief, contractor invoices with work descriptions, final handover certificate confirming fit-out completion, fixed asset register entry, capital vs. expense classification per invoice, lease term confirmation for depreciation period, and store opening date (depreciation start date).

title: How to Record Monthly Depreciation on Retail Store Leasehold Improvements
description: Recognizing one month's depreciation on the store fit-out asset over the lease term.
explanation: An JOD 80,000 fit-out over a 5-year lease generates JOD 1,333/month depreciation — a significant fixed cost that must be covered before the store is profitable.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Depreciation begins on the store opening date (when the asset is available for use) — not the completion date of construction. Set the depreciation period to the shorter of: the remaining lease term, or the asset's physical useful life. Review annually — if the lease is extended, the depreciation period can be extended accordingly. An impairment assessment is required if the store's performance declines significantly.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The depreciation period must not exceed the remaining lease term without a contractually guaranteed renewal. Auditors also check the impairment assessment — a store that is consistently loss-making may have a leasehold improvement asset with a recoverable amount below its net book value, requiring impairment recognition.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Fixed asset register (cost, useful life, depreciation start date, monthly charge), lease agreement confirming term, accumulated depreciation roll-forward, annual useful life review, and impairment assessment for underperforming stores.

title: How to Capitalize a POS Terminal Purchase and Setup Cost
description: Recording the purchase and setup of a point-of-sale hardware system as a fixed asset.
explanation: POS terminals are fixed assets capitalized at cost and depreciated over their useful life (typically 3–5 years).

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Include all directly attributable costs in the capitalized amount: hardware purchase price, installation, and configuration. POS software subscriptions (SaaS model) are separate from the hardware — they are operating expenses, not capital. If the POS software is a one-time perpetual license, capitalize it as a separate intangible asset.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors may ask for evidence that the POS terminals physically exist in the stores — serial numbers in the asset register should match physical tags on the hardware. Software subscription costs incorrectly capitalized alongside hardware inflate fixed assets and understate operating expenses.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: POS hardware invoice (serial numbers, model numbers), installation record, fixed asset register entry with serial numbers, serial number-to-location mapping, and separate treatment of POS software (operating expense or intangible).

title: How to Record Monthly Depreciation on POS Terminal Hardware
description: Amortizing the POS hardware cost over its useful life using straight-line depreciation.
explanation: A JOD 3,500 POS system with a 3-year life generates JOD 97/month depreciation. POS hardware depreciates faster than structural fit-out.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: POS hardware has a useful life of 3–5 years — technology obsolescence often drives replacement before physical failure. Review the useful life annually and accelerate depreciation if replacement is planned. When old POS terminals are replaced, derecognize the old asset (remove cost and accumulated depreciation) and recognize any gain or loss on disposal.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: POS terminals that are fully depreciated but still in use continue to generate revenue without additional depreciation charge — this is correct. Continuing to depreciate a fully amortized asset overstates depreciation expense. Auditors check the accumulated depreciation balance against the total capitalized cost.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Fixed asset register (POS terminals with serial numbers, cost, useful life, accumulated depreciation), annual useful life review, replacement schedule, disposal record for replaced terminals, and depreciation schedule.

title: How to Capitalize Shelving Units, Display Cases, and Store Fixtures
description: Recording significant branded shelving and display fixtures as fixed assets above the capitalization threshold.
explanation: Significant fixtures above the capitalization threshold are fixed assets. Smaller items (hangers, price tags) are expensed immediately as store supplies.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Set a capitalization threshold (e.g., JOD 500 per item or JOD 2,000 per batch of identical items). Fixtures above the threshold are capitalized and depreciated; those below are expensed. Custom-built or brand-standard shelving systems (e.g., franchise-required fixtures) are typically capitalized given their cost and designed lifespan. Maintain a fixture register by store location.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors physically verify fixtures listed in the asset register during store visits. Fixtures that have been removed or replaced should be derecognized. A batch of low-value items purchased together (e.g., 50 hangers at JOD 10 each) may still be below the per-item threshold and should be expensed even though the total is JOD 500.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Fixture supplier invoice, installation record, fixed asset register entry with store location, capitalization threshold policy, annual physical verification, and disposal record for replaced fixtures.

title: How to Record Monthly Depreciation on Store Furniture and Display Fixtures
description: Expensing the monthly wear-and-tear on capitalized retail furniture, display cases, and shelving.
explanation: Retail fixtures are depreciated over 5 years (straight-line). The monthly charge is part of the fixed overhead that management must monitor relative to store sales volume.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Depreciation starts when the fixture is installed and ready for use — not when it is purchased. Group fixtures of the same type and install date into a single asset class for efficiency. Review the useful life assumption annually — fixtures that are replaced more frequently than the original estimate should have their remaining life shortened.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Fully depreciated fixtures still in use have a zero book value but continue to generate value — this is normal and no adjustment is needed. Auditors will check that the accumulated depreciation for fully depreciated assets equals their gross cost. Continuing to depreciate a fully amortized fixture overstates depreciation expense.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Fixed asset register with installation dates and useful lives, accumulated depreciation roll-forward, useful life review memo, and physical asset count confirming fixtures are still in service.

title: How to Record a Store Renovation and Decide Between Capital Expenditure and Expense
description: Correctly expensing a store repaint that restores (not enhances) the asset to its original condition.
explanation: Routine repainting restores the asset to its original condition but does not enhance or extend its life — it is expensed immediately. A full refit adding new lighting or expanding the layout would be capitalized.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The test: does the work restore (expense) or enhance/extend (capitalize)? Repainting existing walls = expense. Adding new lighting tracks and electrical upgrades = capitalize. Replacing worn carpet with identical carpet = expense. Replacing carpet with heated flooring = capitalize. When in doubt, consult with the external auditor before committing to a treatment.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Large renovation invoices near year-end are scrutinized for capitalization avoidance — expensing significant enhancements reduces taxable income in the current year. Auditors will review the renovation scope in detail, often requesting the contractor's specifications. Multiple small renovation invoices from the same contractor over a short period may represent a single project that should be capitalized.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Contractor invoice with detailed scope of work, architect or contractor specifications, capital vs. expense decision memo, Management authorization, and comparison to prior similar projects (precedent for treatment).

title: How to Write Off Fully Depreciated Store Fixtures When They Are Replaced
description: Removing old display shelving from the books when replaced, with no gain or loss since net book value is zero.
explanation: When a fully depreciated asset is disposed of, both the cost and accumulated depreciation are removed. No gain or loss arises since the net book value is zero.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Process the disposal immediately when old fixtures are physically removed — do not leave zero-net-book-value assets in the fixed asset register beyond their disposal date. If there is any residual value realized on disposal (sale of scrap metal, for example), recognize it as a gain (Other Income). Update the physical asset list maintained by the store operations team.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Fixed assets that have been physically disposed of but remain on the register inflate both gross assets and accumulated depreciation — a misstatement. Auditors may conduct physical asset inspections and identify items on the register that no longer exist. A written disposal policy with an authorization process helps prevent this.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Disposal authorization, physical removal record (date, items removed), fixed asset register update, scrap/salvage proceeds (if any) recorded as Other Income, and annual physical asset verification confirming disposed items are removed.

title: How to Prepare and Record the Monthly VAT Output Settlement for Retail Sales in Jordan
description: Summarizing total VAT collected on retail sales and netting against input VAT to determine the ISTD payment.
explanation: Net VAT payable = Output VAT (collected from customers) minus Input VAT (paid on purchases). Only the net difference is remitted to the ISTD monthly.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Run the VAT summary report at month-end from the ERP — total output VAT from all taxable sales minus total input VAT from registered supplier invoices. Verify that the output VAT balance equals exactly 16% of all taxable net sales for the period. Include reverse charge VAT on foreign services in both output and input. File the VAT return and pay by the 30th of the following month.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: ISTD reconciles declared output VAT to declared turnover — if output VAT ÷ 16% does not equal reported taxable revenue, an inquiry follows. Auditors also check that input VAT claims are supported by valid invoices (TRN required). Exempt sales must be clearly separated from taxable sales in the revenue ledger.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Monthly VAT summary report (output and input by category), all supplier VAT invoices for the period, VAT return filed with ISTD, ISTD payment receipt, reconciliation of output VAT to 16% × net taxable sales, and exempt vs. taxable sales breakdown.

title: How to Record Recoverable VAT Input Tax on Inventory Purchases
description: Separating VAT paid on inventory from the net inventory cost as a recoverable input tax asset.
explanation: VAT on inventory is a recoverable asset, not a cost. It is offset against VAT collected on sales when calculating the monthly net VAT payment to the ISTD.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The ERP auto-splits supplier invoices based on the tax code — net cost to inventory, VAT to Input Tax. Never include VAT in the inventory account. Ensure the supplier's TRN appears on every VAT invoice before claiming input tax. Maintain an input tax register by period for VAT return preparation and potential ISTD audit.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Input VAT claims are tested against originating invoices during ISTD audits. Missing TRN numbers, invalid TRNs, or invoices from unregistered suppliers disqualify the input tax claim. Auditors also verify that input VAT on restricted categories (entertainment, passenger vehicles) is appropriately limited or excluded per Jordan's Sales Tax Law.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Supplier VAT invoices (TRN, net, VAT, total, date), VAT Input Tax register, ISTD TRN verification for key suppliers, monthly VAT return showing input claimed, and 5-year invoice archive.

title: How to Record the Monthly VAT Remittance Payment to the ISTD
description: Paying the net VAT liability to the ISTD by the monthly filing deadline.
explanation: This is the final step in the VAT cycle — transferring the collected net VAT to the government. Late payment attracts penalties and interest.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Pay by bank transfer to the ISTD-designated account by the 30th of the following month. Retain the transfer confirmation as evidence of timely payment. After remittance, the Net VAT Payable account should be zero. Keep 5 years of VAT returns and all supporting invoices — ISTD can audit any period within that window.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: ISTD tracks late payments automatically and imposes penalties. Large, irregular, or declining VAT payments relative to prior periods may trigger a full VAT audit. Auditors verify that the payment amount matches the filed return and that all prior VAT liabilities have been settled.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Filed VAT return, bank transfer confirmation to ISTD, ISTD payment receipt or acknowledgment, Net VAT Payable reconciliation to zero, and 5-year archive of all VAT returns and supporting documentation.

title: How to Record a Sale of VAT Exempt or Zero-Rated Goods in Jordan
description: Recording a sale of a product category that is exempt from Jordan's sales tax, with no VAT output collected.
explanation: Exempt goods are sold without adding VAT. No Sales Tax Payable entry is made. Retailers must separate exempt and taxable sales for accurate VAT return filing.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Configure exempt product SKUs with a zero-tax code in the POS so they do not generate output VAT. The POS daily report must separately identify taxable and exempt sales so the VAT return can be accurately filed. Note: if you sell both taxable and exempt goods, your input VAT recovery may be partially restricted (partial exemption rules) — obtain tax advice on the applicable method.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: ISTD auditors verify that sales claimed as exempt are genuinely for exempt product categories. Incorrectly classifying taxable goods as exempt reduces output VAT — a significant underpayment offense. The partial exemption calculation (if applicable) is also scrutinized to ensure input VAT recovery is not overstated on mixed businesses.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: List of exempt product SKUs with legal basis for exemption, POS report separating taxable and exempt sales, VAT return showing both categories, partial exemption calculation (if applicable), and tax advisor opinion confirming exemption eligibility.

title: How to Capitalize Customs Duty on Imported Goods into Inventory Cost
description: Adding import duties paid at customs to the cost of imported inventory as a landed cost under IAS 2.
explanation: Import duties are part of the inventory's landed cost and are capitalized under IAS 2. They increase COGS when items are sold and directly affect the gross margin.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Use a landed cost module in the ERP to include customs duties, port handling fees, and customs clearance agent fees in the inventory cost. Allocate across the items in the shipment using value, weight, or volume. Unlike VAT, customs duties are NOT recoverable — they permanently increase the inventory cost and flow through COGS.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Customs duties must be capitalized into inventory under IAS 2 — expensing them as a period cost is a misstatement. Auditors test landed cost allocations for large import shipments. The customs clearance declaration is the primary supporting document for the duty amount.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Customs clearance declaration (showing duty rates and amounts), customs payment receipt, landed cost allocation calculation (duty per SKU), inventory receiving record showing updated unit cost, and customs agent invoice.

title: How to Accrue the Year-End Corporate Income Tax Provision for a Retail Business
description: Recognizing the estimated income tax liability on the retail store's taxable profit at year-end.
explanation: Income tax is accrued based on taxable profit. Differences between accounting profit and taxable income create deferred tax assets or liabilities.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The income tax provision requires a tax computation prepared with the tax advisor: accounting profit adjusted for non-deductible items (fines, unsupported expenses, excessive entertainment), tax allowances (accelerated depreciation), and loss carryforwards. The resulting taxable income × the Jordanian corporate tax rate = current tax provision. Assess whether deferred tax assets or liabilities arise from timing differences.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Income tax provisions are always scrutinized. Key retail-specific risks: (1) COGS overstated by unsupported shrinkage or obsolescence — ISTD may add back, (2) Rent paid to individual landlords where WHT was not withheld — creates additional liability, (3) Staff expenses without documentation — disallowed by ISTD, (4) Depreciation exceeding ISTD's prescribed rates — timing difference creating deferred tax liability.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Tax computation (accounting to taxable profit bridge), ISTD depreciation rate schedule, prior year tax returns, WHT remittance records, non-deductible items schedule, deferred tax calculation, and tax advisor sign-off.

title: How to Record the Annual Municipality Trade License Fee as a Prepaid Asset
description: Paying the annual commercial operating license and municipality fees, amortized monthly over the license period.
explanation: Annual licenses are prepaid assets amortized monthly. Without a valid trade license, the store cannot legally operate.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Record all annual government fees (trade license, health and safety permits, civil defense certificate) as prepaid assets on payment date. Amortize monthly over the license period. Maintain a license renewal calendar with responsible owners — operating with an expired license risks immediate closure by the municipality and reputational damage. Cross-reference license fees to the physical license certificate.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that licenses are current — expired licenses mean the store was technically operating illegally during the expired period. License fees for prior periods (late renewals, penalties) should not be capitalized — they are period expenses. ISTD may also check that the business address on the license matches the actual store address.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Trade license certificate (period covered, premises address), payment receipt, prepaid amortization schedule, license renewal calendar, and copies of all current valid licenses.

title: How to Withhold and Record the 5% Rent Tax When Paying an Individual Landlord in Jordan
description: Deducting 5% withholding tax from rent paid to an individual (non-corporate) landlord and remitting to ISTD.
explanation: Jordanian law requires a company to deduct 5% from rent paid to an individual landlord and remit it to the ISTD on their behalf.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Set up the WHT calculation automatically in the AP module when the landlord is flagged as an individual. Issue a withholding certificate to the landlord each month. Remit to ISTD by the 10th of the following month using Form 103. If the landlord is a company (has a TIN), no WHT is required — verify landlord status before applying.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Failure to withhold rent tax from individual landlords is a top ISTD enforcement area. The full WHT liability (not just penalties) falls on the tenant who failed to withhold. Auditors check the landlord's status for every rental agreement — a lease with an individual that shows no WHT deduction is an immediate finding. Issue annual WHT certificates to landlords to document compliance.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement with landlord identification (individual vs. company), landlord National ID or TIN, monthly WHT deduction records, ISTD remittance receipts (Form 103), annual WHT certificate issued to landlord, and landlord bank account records confirming net payment.

title: How to Record Monthly Bank Account and POS Terminal Maintenance Charges
description: Expensing recurring bank account maintenance fees and POS terminal rental charges found on the monthly statement.
explanation: POS terminal rental and bank service fees are recurring operating costs, typically discovered during bank reconciliation.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Bank and POS fees are auto-debited and identified during the monthly bank reconciliation. Separate the POS terminal rental from transaction-based processing fees in the chart of accounts — the rental is fixed, while processing fees are variable. Track the combined cost of banking services as a percentage of total card sales to assess whether the POS arrangement is competitive.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Unexpected fee increases should be queried with the bank immediately — they may represent unauthorized charges or rate changes that should have been pre-negotiated. Auditors verify that fees are within the merchant agreement and that the bank reconciliation captures all charges.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Bank statement showing fees, merchant agreement confirming fee schedule, bank reconciliation, Bank & Finance Charges Expense ledger, and investigation records for unexpected fee increases.

title: How to Record the End-of-Day Cash Count and Night Safe Deposit
description: Transferring the day's cash takings from the store till to the bank account, moving between two asset accounts.
explanation: The daily deposit transfers cash between two asset accounts — from the physical till to the bank account. This is not a revenue or expense event.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: This is a pure balance sheet transfer — no P&L impact. The Cash in Hand account should reflect only the float remaining after the deposit (e.g., JOD 150 float for change). The deposit amount should match the POS Z-report net cash sales less the retained float. Any discrepancy is a Cash Over/Short entry (separate entry). The bank will typically credit the deposit the next business day — check for timing differences in the bank reconciliation.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors will reconcile Cash in Hand at the year-end balance sheet date to confirm only the approved float amount remains. A large Cash in Hand balance at year-end (suggesting deposits were not made) is a significant cash management control weakness. Missing deposit records for specific days may indicate unreported cash sales.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Daily cash count sheet (signed by cashier and manager), POS Z-report for the day, bank deposit slip, bank statement confirming receipt of deposit the following day, and Cash in Hand float policy document.

title: How to Record a Bank Overdraft Used for Short-Term Working Capital
description: Recording the use of an overdraft facility to pay suppliers when the bank balance is negative during a slow trading period.
explanation: When the bank balance goes negative, the liability shifts from Accounts Payable to Bank Overdraft. The bank charges interest on the overdrawn balance.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Configure the ERP to reclassify a negative bank account balance to Bank Overdraft Payable (current liability) — a negative asset presentation is incorrect under IFRS. The overdraft is a current liability and should be classified as such on the balance sheet. Accrue interest on the overdraft monthly based on the outstanding balance and the bank's overdraft interest rate.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Bank overdrafts must be disclosed separately from positive bank balances on the balance sheet unless there is a legal right of set-off with another account at the same bank. Covenant breaches on the overdraft facility (minimum balance, maximum draw) that give the bank the right to demand repayment may cause reclassification from current to immediately payable.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Bank overdraft facility agreement (limit, interest rate, covenants), bank statement confirming the overdraft balance, Bank Overdraft Payable GL entry, monthly interest accrual, and covenant compliance confirmation.

title: How to Record a Trade Finance Credit Line Drawdown for Seasonal Inventory Purchasing
description: Using a revolving inventory finance facility to fund large seasonal stock purchases without tying up operating cash.
explanation: Inventory credit lines allow retailers to stock up for peak seasons without tying up their own cash. The facility is repaid as stock is sold, matching the cash flow to the sales cycle.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Record the drawdown as a current liability (Trade Finance Facility Payable). The interest accrues separately and is expensed monthly. As seasonal stock sells, repay the facility — the cash flow from sales funds the repayment.
