practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Fund balance policy adopted by governing body, list of restricted fund balance items with legal citations, committed fund balance ordinances/resolutions with dates, assignment authority documentation, fund balance classification workpaper.

title: Enterprise Fund - Utility Billing Revenue (Water / Sewer / Electric)
description: Recording monthly utility service revenue in a municipal water or sewer enterprise fund, recognized under full accrual basis (same as proprietary accounting) when service is delivered.
explanation: Enterprise Funds (utility, transit, airports, parking) use full accrual accounting — like private sector businesses — NOT modified accrual. Revenue is recognized when service is delivered, expenses when incurred, and capital assets are capitalized and depreciated. Enterprise funds report a Statement of Net Position (balance sheet), Statement of Revenues, Expenses, and Changes in Fund Net Position (income statement), and Statement of Cash Flows. Utility revenue is recognized based on meter readings and actual consumption, with an accrual for the unbilled period at month-end.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Utility billing systems (Tyler Incode, Infinite Visions, Harris Utility) interface with the general ledger to post billing revenue. Unbilled revenue (service delivered between the last meter read date and fiscal year-end) must be estimated and accrued at year-end. This 'cycle billing' accrual is often a significant amount.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test the unbilled revenue accrual methodology (estimated days of unbilled consumption × average daily billing rate). Rate compliance is verified — rates must be established by ordinance or resolution. Water loss rates (non-revenue water) are reviewed for reasonableness.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Utility billing system reports, rate schedule approved by governing body, meter read reports, unbilled revenue accrual calculation, accounts receivable aging by customer class, bad debt write-off documentation.

title: Enterprise Fund - System Development / Connection Fee Revenue
description: Recording system development charges (SDCs) or connection fees paid by new utility customers for the right to connect to the government's water/sewer system, with revenue deferral analysis.
explanation: Connection fees / SDCs represent the new customer's share of existing system capacity. Under GASB 33, these are exchange transactions recognized when the connection right is granted (point in time). However, some governments treat a portion as deferred revenue if there is an ongoing performance obligation (providing capacity over the service life). SDC revenue is often restricted to capacity expansion projects by state law — unrestricted spending of SDC revenue is a legal violation in many states.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track SDC revenue separately by meter size and service type. SDC rates must be supported by a rate study (cost of facility analysis or system buy-in analysis) that demonstrates the nexus between the fee and the actual cost of capacity. Many states require SDC updates at least every 5 years. Restriction on use of SDC funds must be enforced — maintain separate cash accounts or sub-ledgers for SDC balances.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The legal nexus between connection fees and capacity costs is subject to legal challenge. Auditors verify fee computation methodology and compliance with state SDC statutes. Spending SDC funds on operating costs (not capital) is a legal violation and a material audit finding.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: SDC rate study (cost of facility or system buy-in analysis), fee schedule adopted by ordinance, new customer connection permits, SDC segregated account tracking, capital expenditure documentation for SDC-funded projects, state SDC statute compliance.

title: Enterprise Fund - Capital Asset Depreciation (Full Accrual)
description: Recording annual depreciation on enterprise fund capital assets (water treatment plant, distribution pipes, sewer lines) using straight-line depreciation over infrastructure useful lives.
explanation: Enterprise funds use full accrual accounting — capital assets are depreciated over their useful lives. Utility infrastructure typically has very long lives: water mains 50–100 years, treatment plants 30–50 years, pumping stations 25–40 years. Unlike governmental funds (where capital outlay is an expenditure), enterprise fund capital assets appear on the balance sheet and are depreciated annually. The depreciation expense reduces net position over time but represents the consumption of capital investment.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Enterprise fund fixed asset modules must be comprehensive — water and sewer systems often have thousands of individual asset components (each segment of pipe, each pump, each meter). Componentized depreciation (tracking components separately) is required for major infrastructure to properly account for partial replacements. Many utilities use GIS-integrated asset management systems.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Enterprise fund infrastructure assets are often among the largest items on a government's balance sheet. Auditors test the completeness of the capital asset register and the appropriateness of useful lives — particularly for aging infrastructure where actual remaining life may be less than the standard useful life. Asset condition-based depreciation is an emerging approach.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Enterprise fund capital asset register, useful life policy by asset type, depreciation schedule by asset class, infrastructure map corroborating asset count, capital asset note roll-forward (cost and accumulated depreciation).

title: Enterprise Fund - Rate Stabilization Reserve Restriction of Net Position
description: Recording the designation of enterprise fund net position as 'restricted for rate stabilization,' providing a reserve to absorb revenue shortfalls without immediate rate increases.

entries.account: Net Position - Restricted for Rate Stabilization

explanation: Rate stabilization reserves are established by utility enterprise funds to smooth rate increases over time. When fund performance is strong, net position is transferred to the rate stabilization reserve. During revenue shortfalls, the reserve absorbs the shortfall without requiring immediate customer rate increases. Under GASB 34 / GASB 62, this is reported as a restriction of net position (not a separate fund). The reserve mechanism requires formal adoption by the governing body and documented drawdown criteria.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The restriction is an accounting reclassification within net position — it does not involve a separate bank account (though some utilities do segregate the cash). The board resolution establishing the reserve and drawdown criteria must be documented. The rate stabilization balance is disclosed in the net position note.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that rate stabilization reserve restrictions are authorized by the governing body and that drawdowns are made per the established criteria. Reserves established by management without governing body action may not meet the 'restricted' classification threshold.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Board resolution establishing rate stabilization reserve, reserve balance and drawdown history, rate stabilization criteria documentation, GASB 34 net position restriction disclosure in notes.

title: Enterprise Fund - Revenue Bond Debt Service Coverage Ratio Compliance
description: Calculating and documenting the annual debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) required by revenue bond indentures, typically a minimum of 1.25x net revenues to annual debt service.

entries.account: Net Revenues Available for Debt Service (Operating Revenue - O&M)

explanation: Revenue bonds (issued by enterprise funds — utilities, airports, convention centers) are not backed by the government's taxing power. They are secured solely by enterprise revenues. Bond indentures typically require a minimum debt service coverage ratio (net revenues / annual debt service ≥ 1.20x–1.50x). Falling below the minimum coverage triggers bond covenants — the government may be required to hire a rate consultant, increase rates, or face technical default. The DSCR calculation must be performed annually and certified to the bond trustee.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The DSCR calculation follows the specific definition in the bond indenture — 'net revenues' may include or exclude depreciation, rate stabilization transfers, or other items depending on the indenture definition. Do not assume accounting net income = bond indenture net revenues. Calculate per the indenture definition precisely. Flag DSCR covenant risk as part of the year-end close process.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Revenue bond covenant compliance is tested annually by auditors. The bond trustee may also independently calculate the DSCR. Covenant violations must be disclosed in the financial statements. Auditors will flag ratios approaching the minimum covenant level as a going concern risk indicator.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Revenue bond indenture (DSCR definition), DSCR calculation per indenture definition, certified revenue report to bond trustee, rate history and projection showing continued covenant compliance, bond counsel opinion on covenant compliance.

title: GASB 87 Lease - Lessee Right-to-Use Asset and Lease Liability Recognition
description: Recording the right-to-use (ROU) intangible asset and corresponding lease liability when a government enters into a lease as a lessee under GASB 87 (effective FY2022).
explanation: GASB 87 (effective for fiscal years beginning after June 15, 2021) fundamentally changed lease accounting for governments — replacing GASB 13 and 62. Under GASB 87, lessees recognize an intangible right-to-use (ROU) asset and a corresponding lease liability for virtually all leases with a maximum possible term exceeding 12 months. The ROU asset is an intangible asset (not property/equipment) amortized over the shorter of the lease term or asset's useful life. This eliminated the operating/capital lease distinction — ALL leases (with minor exceptions) are on-balance-sheet. Common government leases: office space, vehicles, copiers, equipment.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: GASB 87 adoption required governments to inventory ALL leases and determine measurement dates. The lease liability = present value of future lease payments, discounted at the government's incremental borrowing rate (IBR). The IBR determination for governments (which don't have commercial borrowing activity) required specific guidance — typically the rate on the most recent GO bond issuance. Many governments used a GASB 87 implementation tool or spreadsheet model.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: GASB 87 adoption is still being reviewed for complete and accurate implementation (many governments adopted it for FY2022). Common implementation errors: missing leases (equipment leases, facility leases across departments), incorrect IBR, incorrect lease term (not including reasonably certain renewal options), and incorrect classification of short-term leases. Auditors request a complete lease inventory and test key assumptions.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease inventory (all contracts identified and evaluated), lease calculation worksheets (PV of payments by lease), IBR determination memo, GASB 87 note disclosure, short-term lease exemption documentation, lease terms summary by lease.

title: GASB 87 Lease - Lessor Revenue Recognition (Government as Landlord)
description: Recording lease receivable and deferred inflow when a government is the LESSOR of property (e.g., leasing city-owned space to a tenant or concessionaire) under GASB 87.
explanation: Under GASB 87, when a government is the lessor, it records a Lease Receivable (the present value of future lease payments receivable) and a corresponding Deferred Inflow. The deferred inflow is recognized as revenue over the lease term as payments are received and/or as time passes. Unlike the lessee side, the lessor retains the underlying asset on its balance sheet (the leased property continues to be reported as a capital asset, just identified as 'being leased'). Common government lessor arrangements: airport concession leases, marina slip rentals, stadium leases, ground leases.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track each lease receivable in the ERP with an amortization schedule showing the interest revenue component and principal reduction. The underlying capital asset (leased property) must continue to be depreciated and reported in the capital asset register with a notation that it is subject to a lease.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Governments often overlook their lessor position — particularly for informal space-sharing arrangements that constitute GASB 87 leases. Auditors request a listing of all arrangements where the government allows other entities to use government-owned space in exchange for consideration. The deferred inflow recognition pattern must be consistent with the lease payment schedule.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement (government as lessor), lease receivable calculation (PV of future payments), deferred inflow amortization schedule, underlying capital asset identification in capital asset register, GASB 87 lessor note disclosures.

title: GASB 96 - Subscription-Based IT Arrangement (SBITA) Right-to-Use Asset
description: Recording the right-to-use intangible asset and subscription liability for a government's subscription to cloud-based software or SaaS (Software as a Service) under GASB 96.
explanation: GASB 96 (effective FY2023) applies lease-like accounting to subscription-based IT arrangements — cloud computing, SaaS, PaaS, IaaS — where the government controls the right to use IT assets. Like GASB 87 leases, governments recognize a right-to-use intangible asset and corresponding subscription liability measured at the present value of future subscription payments. Common examples: ERP cloud subscriptions (Tyler Munis SaaS, Oracle Cloud), cloud data storage, software-as-a-service applications. Arrangements with terms ≤12 months are exempt.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Inventory all cloud and SaaS subscriptions across all departments — many go undetected because technology subscriptions are often paid by credit card across departments without central IT oversight. Determine which subscriptions qualify under GASB 96 (government controls use, not just a right to receive service from the vendor's pool). The measurement is PV of future subscription payments at the IBR.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: GASB 96 is very recently effective and many governments are still implementing. Auditors request a SBITA inventory and evaluate whether all significant subscriptions have been identified and measured. IT contracts that include both subscription and service elements require bifurcation — only the subscription element is on-balance-sheet.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: SBITA inventory (all cloud/SaaS contracts evaluated), GASB 96 vs. service contract determination memo, SBITA calculation worksheets (PV of subscription payments), IBR determination, GASB 96 note disclosures, short-term SBITA exemptions.

title: Special Assessment - Levy for Neighborhood Infrastructure Project
description: Recording a special assessment levy against properties in an assessment district for their proportionate share of neighborhood infrastructure improvements (sidewalks, streetlights, drainage).

entries.account: Deferred Inflows - Special Assessments (Not Yet Available)
Special Assessment Revenue (Current Year Installment - Available)

explanation: Special assessments are levies against benefiting properties for specific improvements. Unlike property taxes (ad valorem), special assessments are based on benefit received. The full levy is recorded as a receivable but only the current installment (due within the year plus the 60-day availability window) is recognized as revenue — the multi-year installment portion is deferred. If the government is obligated in some manner for the related debt (special assessment bonds), both the liability and the receivable appear in the government's statements.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track special assessments by district and parcel. Annual installments typically include principal and interest components. The interest component is revenue as accrued; the principal reduces the receivable. Property liens securing the assessment must be recorded and maintained until paid.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors assess the collectibility of special assessments — if the assessed improvements don't add value to the property, collection rates may be low. The government's obligation on related special assessment debt (full faith and credit vs. special assessment bonds with no government guaranty) determines the extent of disclosure in the financial statements.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Assessment district formation ordinance, engineer's report (benefit analysis and cost allocation), assessment roll (levy per parcel), installment payment schedule, property lien filings, deferred inflows schedule.

title: Compensated Absences - Vacation & Sick Leave Liability (GASB 101)
description: Recording the accrued liability for compensated absences (vacation leave, sick leave, and similar benefits) under GASB 101, with recognition at current salary rates for leave expected to result in payments.

entries.account: Expenditures - Compensated Absences (Governmental Fund - Current Portion)

explanation: GASB 101 (effective FY2024) updated compensated absence accounting. The new standard requires recognizing a liability for leave that (1) has been earned by the employee, (2) has accumulated (can be carried forward), and (3) will be paid. Sick leave is now recognized as a liability when it is probable the employee will use it as pay upon termination or retirement — a departure from the old 'will vest' approach. In governmental funds, only the current maturity (due within the current period) is reported as a fund liability. The full long-term balance appears only in the government-wide statements.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The compensated absence liability requires data from the HR/payroll system (employee leave balances by type, by employee) multiplied by current salary rates (GASB 101 requires current salary rates, not historical rates). Calculate the full liability for government-wide statements; determine the current portion (expected to be paid within 12 months) for the governmental fund statements.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test the compensated absence liability by selecting a sample of employees, tracing their leave balances to payroll records, and recalculating the liability at current rates. New GASB 101 sick leave probability of payout analysis requires management's estimation of employee turnover and sick leave usage patterns — these estimates are a key audit focus.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Payroll system leave balance report (all employees, all leave types), current salary rate list, compensated absence liability calculation workpaper, GASB 101 probability analysis for sick leave, rollforward of liability (beginning balance + accruals - payments = ending balance), note disclosure.

title: Tax Increment Financing (TIF) - Increment Revenue Capture
description: Recording property tax increment revenue captured in a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district, representing the increase in property tax revenue above the base year value within the TIF area.

entries.account: Property Tax Revenue - TIF Increment (Special Revenue Fund)

explanation: TIF districts capture the incremental property tax revenue (above the frozen base year assessed value) generated within the district to finance economic development infrastructure. The 'base' property taxes flow to the normal taxing bodies (city, county, school district). The 'increment' flows to the TIF fund to repay TIF bonds or pay for development costs. The TIF creates complex accounting because: (1) general tax revenue is reduced by the TIF increment, and (2) GASB 77 requires disclosure of tax abatements that include TIF agreements.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: TIF districts require a separate Special Revenue Fund to account for increment revenues and TIF project expenditures. Track the base vs. increment assessed value annually as the assessor revalues properties. TIF bond debt appears in the government's debt disclosures. GASB 77 requires disclosure of the annual revenue forgone due to TIF (which reduces available property taxes to other taxing bodies).
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: TIF accounting errors are common: (1) failing to reduce general fund property tax by the TIF increment, (2) not disclosing TIF abatements under GASB 77, (3) improper expenditures from TIF funds (only eligible project costs within the TIF boundary). Each state has specific TIF statutes governing eligible expenditures.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: TIF district formation ordinance, assessed valuation comparison (base year vs. current), increment calculation by parcel, TIF fund financial statements, TIF bond documents, GASB 77 abatement disclosure calculation, annual TIF report (required in many states).

title: Claims & Judgments - Accrual of Tort/Litigation Liability (GASB 62)
description: Accruing the long-term liability for pending claims and judgments against the government (personal injury, property damage, employment claims) when loss is probable and estimable.
explanation: Governments face ongoing tort liability (slip-and-fall on public property, police misconduct, vehicle accidents, employment discrimination). Under GASB 62 (incorporating SFAS 5 guidance), a liability is accrued when loss is probable and can be reasonably estimated. The liability includes both reported claims (known cases) and IBNR (incurred but not reported) claims, estimated actuarially. In governmental funds, only the current maturity (expected payment within 12 months) appears as a fund liability — the long-term portion is only in government-wide statements. Many governments use a Self-Insurance Internal Service Fund to manage this liability.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The claims and judgments liability calculation requires input from the government's risk management office and outside legal counsel. For governments with significant claim volumes, an actuarial study is needed to estimate IBNR claims. Self-insured governments should maintain a risk management information system (RMIS) tracking all open claims, reserves, and payments.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors send legal confirmation letters to all legal counsel representing the government. Risk management officer inquiry and review of claims register are required. IBNR estimate methodology must be reasonable and consistently applied. Undisclosed large settlements after year-end are a subsequent events matter.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Claims register (open cases with reserve estimates), legal counsel response to audit confirmation letters, actuarial study for IBNR estimate (if material), risk management fund reserves, self-insurance coverage limits and excess insurance policies, rollforward of claims liability.

title: Landfill Closure & Post-Closure Costs - GASB 18 Liability Accrual
description: Accruing the closure and post-closure care liability for a government-owned municipal solid waste landfill based on the capacity used to date relative to total capacity.
explanation: GASB 18 requires governments operating municipal solid waste landfills to accrue estimated closure and post-closure care costs based on the portion of landfill capacity used to date. If the landfill is 40% full, 40% of total estimated closure costs are accrued. Closure costs include: installing the final cover, monitoring systems, and leachate collection. Post-closure costs include: 30-year EPA-required monitoring, groundwater testing, methane monitoring, and maintenance. These are massive long-term liabilities — closure and post-closure can cost $5M–$50M+ for large facilities.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The accrual rate changes annually as more capacity is used. Obtain an annual engineering estimate of total closure and post-closure costs in current dollars. Recalculate the accrual percentage (used capacity / total capacity) and update the liability. Track the liability separately from other long-term liabilities in the notes.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: GASB 18 is frequently underimplemented — many governments operating landfills either don't accrue the liability at all or use outdated engineering estimates. Auditors require a current engineering study supporting the cost estimates. EPA compliance status of the landfill is reviewed — non-compliant landfills have higher estimated costs.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Landfill capacity determination (total design capacity, used capacity), current engineering estimate of closure and post-closure costs, EPA post-closure care permit, state environmental regulatory correspondence, GASB 18 accrual calculation, note disclosure with key assumptions.

title: GASB 34 Reconciliation - Governmental Fund Balance to Government-Wide Net Position
description: Preparing the required reconciliation between total governmental funds fund balance and government-wide net position, explaining all differences arising from the use of different accounting bases.

entries.account: Add: Capital Assets Net of Accumulated Depreciation
Add/Less: Deferred Outflows and Inflows (Pension, OPEB, Refundings)
Add: Internal Service Fund Net Assets

explanation: GASB 34 requires governments to present a reconciliation between governmental fund balance and government-wide net position on the face of the financial statements. This reconciliation is THE most government-specific accounting document that does not exist in private sector accounting. The major reconciling items are: (1) Capital assets not reported in fund statements (+), (2) Long-term debt not reported in fund statements (-), (3) Pension/OPEB liabilities (-), (4) Deferred outflows/inflows (+/-), (5) Internal service fund net assets (+), (6) Deferred inflows in fund statements that are revenue in government-wide (+), (7) Compensated absences long-term portion (-). This reconciliation proves that the two sets of statements agree despite using different measurement focuses.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The reconciliation workpaper is typically prepared in a spreadsheet that documents each line item with its source (capital asset note, long-term debt schedule, pension allocation, etc.). Each line must tie to a specific supporting workpaper. This is often the last workpaper completed in year-end close because it aggregates data from all other areas.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The reconciliation is one of the highest-priority audit procedures for government auditors. Auditors agree each reconciling item to the supporting schedule. Unexplained differences between the reconciliation total and the government-wide net position on the Statement of Net Position are a material error. Common errors: missing reconciling items, double-counting, wrong signs.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Governmental funds balance sheet (total fund balance), capital asset note roll-forward (net of depreciation), long-term debt schedule, pension allocation (GASB 68 data), OPEB liability (GASB 75 data), deferred outflows/inflows schedules, compensated absences long-term schedule, internal service fund balance sheet, completed reconciliation workpaper.

title: Tax Abatement Disclosure - GASB 77 Property Tax Abatement for Economic Development
description: Recording and disclosing a property tax abatement agreement with a business as required by GASB 77, showing the annual revenue forgone by the government to attract/retain economic development.

entries.account: Property Tax Receivable (Full Levy before Abatement)

explanation: GASB 77 (effective 2016) requires governments to disclose tax abatements — agreements where the government reduces or eliminates a company's tax liability in exchange for specific actions (job creation, capital investment, facility construction). Governments must disclose: the abatement program name, purpose, authority, commitment made by the recipient, provisions for recapture (clawback), total dollar amount of taxes abated during the year. Significant abatement agreements with individual companies may require individual-level disclosure.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Develop a process to identify all tax abatement agreements annually. Many abatements are administered by economic development agencies or assessment offices — finance departments may not automatically learn of new agreements. Create an abatement agreement register tracking: company name (if disclosable), program, annual abatement amount, remaining term, and clawback provisions.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: GASB 77 disclosures are tested by auditors against the government's abatement agreement register. Missing abatement disclosures are a common finding — particularly TIF abatements, enterprise zone abatements, and individual company-specific agreements. Auditors will request the complete list of all active abatement agreements.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: All active abatement agreements, annual abatement calculation by agreement, economic development authority notifications, GASB 77 note disclosure workpaper, abatement register by program and recipient, clawback recapture tracking.

title: Custodial Fund - Tax Collection on Behalf of Other Governments (Pass-Through)
description: Recording property tax collections by a county on behalf of multiple taxing districts (cities, schools, special districts), maintaining the funds as a custodial (fiduciary) fund until remittance.

entries.account: Cash - Custodial Fund (Taxes Collected for Others)
Custodial Liability - Taxes Held for Other Governments

explanation: County treasurers typically collect property taxes for ALL taxing bodies within the county (city, county, school districts, fire districts, library districts, etc.) in a single billing. The taxes collected for other taxing bodies are NOT the county's revenues — they are held in a Custodial Fund (formerly Agency Fund) and remitted to the appropriate taxing body on a periodic basis (monthly, quarterly). The county never recognizes these taxes as revenue or expenditure — only as an asset and corresponding liability until remitted.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Maintain separate custodial fund accounting for each taxing body. The remittance schedule must match the tax collection cycle and state law requirements. Delays in remittance to school districts or other taxing bodies can cause significant cash flow problems for those entities and may violate state statutes.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors reconcile custodial fund balances to amounts owed to each taxing body. Unexplained discrepancies may indicate improper commingling with county operating funds or delayed remittances. The custodial fund balance sheet should show zero net position (assets = liabilities) since all collected funds belong to others.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Tax collection and remittance schedule by taxing body, custodial fund bank statement, remittance records by taxing body and by month, reconciliation of tax roll to collections and remittances, written remittance schedule.

title: Custodial Fund - Remittance of Collected Taxes to Other Taxing Bodies
description: Recording the remittance of property taxes held in the custodial fund to their respective taxing bodies (school district, city, fire district, library district).

entries.account: Custodial Liability - Taxes Held for School District
Custodial Liability - Taxes Held for City
Custodial Liability - Taxes Held for Fire District

explanation: Upon remittance, the county's custodial fund liability decreases and cash is disbursed to the respective taxing bodies. Each taxing body records the receipt as property tax revenue in its own fund accounting system. The county's custodial fund has no income statement — only additions and deductions to/from custodial assets (shown in the Statement of Changes in Fiduciary Net Position for custodial funds per GASB 84).

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Wire transfers to each taxing body should be traceable to the specific tax levy period and taxing body. Generate remittance advices for each taxing body showing the breakdown of the payment by levy type and property tax year. Some states require remittance of interest earned on tax collections to the respective taxing bodies.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors reconcile remittances to collection records and confirm amounts with recipient taxing bodies (inter-entity confirmation). Interest earned on tax collections while held in the custodial fund must be allocated and remitted per state law — retention of this interest by the county is a common finding.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Remittance calculation by taxing body and levy year, wire transfer confirmations, remittance advices sent to each taxing body, interest calculation on held balances, state law compliance for interest remittance, confirmations from recipient taxing bodies.

title: Property Tax Sale - Delinquent Tax Certificate Sale
description: Recording the sale of delinquent tax certificates to private investors (tax lien certificates), converting uncollectible tax receivables to immediate cash while transferring collection risk.
explanation: Many states allow governments to sell delinquent tax receivables to private investors (tax lien certificates or tax deeds). The investor pays the government the face amount of taxes owed (less a discount) and earns interest from the delinquent property owner. The government derecognizes the receivable and the corresponding allowance, recognizes cash received, and recognizes a gain or loss (proceeds vs. net receivable). This provides immediate cash but forfeits the interest and penalty income.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track tax liens sold by parcel in the property tax module. The lien remains on the parcel and must be tracked for potential tax deed proceedings if the owner fails to redeem. GASB guidance on tax lien transfers treats the transaction as a sale (receivable derecognized) only if the government has transferred substantially all risks and rewards to the investor.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors assess whether the tax lien transfer qualifies as a sale (and thus derecognition of the receivable) or remains an obligation of the government. If the government has agreed to repurchase uncollected liens, it may need to retain the receivable on its balance sheet. The discount rate from face value is scrutinized.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Tax lien certificate purchase agreement, list of parcels transferred (with delinquent amounts), closing settlement statement, state tax lien sale statute compliance, gain/loss calculation, updated delinquent tax roll after lien sale.

title: Developer Contribution - Cash Contribution for Off-Site Infrastructure
description: Recording a cash contribution from a private developer for off-site infrastructure improvements (road widening, intersection improvements) required as a condition of development approval.

entries.account: Cash & Cash Equivalents - Capital Projects Fund

explanation: Developer contributions (impact fees, exaction fees, off-site improvement funds) are paid by private developers as a condition of land use approval. Under GASB 33, these are non-exchange transactions. Revenue is recognized when all eligibility requirements are met — typically when the capital expenditure for which the contribution is intended is made. Until the qualifying expenditure occurs, the contribution is a Deferred Inflow. Restricted developer contributions must be tracked separately and spent on the designated project per the development agreement.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Maintain a developer contribution register by development agreement, showing: contribution amount, intended project, expiration date (if applicable), and amounts expended. Contributions not spent within a specified period may be refundable to the developer under some state laws. Track in the Capital Projects Fund.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that developer contributions are spent on the designated improvements, not on general government purposes. Unspent contributions held for years may be refundable and create a liability (if the development agreement's improvement deadline has passed). The deferred inflow recognition must align with the actual infrastructure expenditure.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Development agreement specifying contribution purpose and timing, payment receipt, project expenditure tracking, deferred inflow recognition schedule, development agreement expiration dates, refund provisions.

title: Special Item - Sale of Government-Owned Land (Unusual & Infrequent)
description: Recording the sale of a significant parcel of government-owned land as a Special Item — separately disclosed in the Statement of Activities because it is within management's control, significant, and unusual or infrequent.

entries.account: Special Item - Gain on Sale of Land (Below Net Position)

explanation: GASB 34 defines Special Items as transactions within management's control that are either unusual in nature or infrequent in occurrence. They are presented BELOW the normal change in net position line (but ABOVE net position) in the Statement of Activities — separately from ordinary revenues and expenses. Examples: significant land sales, sale of a government building, one-time debt forgiveness, extraordinary environmental remediation. Extraordinary Items (outside management's control AND unusual AND infrequent) are even further separated. This separation prevents one-time gains from obscuring operating performance trends.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Identify and disclose special items as they arise during the year. The classification (special item vs. extraordinary item vs. ordinary revenue) requires judgment based on the specific facts and GASB 34 definitions. Consult with auditors before finalizing the classification of significant unusual transactions.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors assess whether transactions are properly classified as special items and whether the presentation complies with GASB 34. Significant land sales or asset disposals that are buried in ordinary revenues/expenditures rather than disclosed as special items are a presentation finding.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Land sale agreement and closing statement, appraisal of land sold, GASB 34 classification memo (ordinary vs. special vs. extraordinary), board approval of sale, title transfer documentation, net book value calculation from fixed asset register.

title: Property Tax Refund - Abatement or Assessment Appeal Refund
description: Recording the refund of property taxes previously collected when an assessment appeal is successful or an abatement application is granted by the board of review.
explanation: Property owners have the right to appeal assessments or apply for abatements. When an appeal or abatement is granted, the government must refund the excess taxes collected. Under modified accrual, the refund is a reduction of current year revenue (if the overassessment relates to the current year) or a prior period adjustment if it relates to prior years' taxes already recognized as revenue. If the refund is large enough to be material, it may require disclosure in the notes as a subsequent event or contingent liability.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track pending assessment appeals and abatement applications in a contingency register. Estimate the probability and amount of successful appeals for financial statement accrual purposes. Large assessments under appeal (commercial/industrial properties) can represent material contingent refunds. Some governments purchase appeal insurance.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors request the pending appeals list from the assessor and board of review. Material pending refunds that are probable are accrued as liabilities. The adequacy of the refund reserve (often included in the uncollectible tax allowance) is assessed. High assessment appeal rates may indicate systemic assessment quality issues.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Assessment appeal and abatement application register, board of review/appeals tribunal decisions, refund calculation by case, refund check/ACH payment records, contingent liability assessment memo for pending appeals.

title: Pension Trust Fund - Investment Income, Fair Value Changes (GASB 31/67)
description: Recording investment income (interest, dividends, and net change in fair value) within the pension trust fund, reflecting the actuarial significance of investment returns on pension plan funding status.

entries.account: Interest and Dividend Income - Pension Investments
Net Change in Fair Value of Investments - Pension

explanation: Investment returns are the most critical determinant of pension plan funding status — a 1% change in the long-term expected rate of return assumption can change the actuarial liability by hundreds of millions for large plans. All investments in the pension trust are carried at fair value per GASB 31/72, with all unrealized and realized gains/losses flowing through the trust's income statement as 'Additions.' The investment return is compared to the long-term expected rate (typically 6.5%–7.5% for public pension plans) in the actuarial valuation.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The pension trust investment portfolio typically includes domestic and international equities, fixed income, alternative investments (private equity, real estate, hedge funds), and cash equivalents. Fair value measurement for illiquid alternatives (private equity, real estate) requires quarterly or annual appraisals. Investment manager fee disclosure (GASB 67 requires total investment expense) is required.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Pension trust investment fair values are high-risk audit areas, particularly for alternative investments (Level 3 in the fair value hierarchy). Auditors use investment specialists to evaluate alternative asset valuations. The actual investment return vs. the assumed rate has direct implications for the employer's NPL — significantly below expected returns increase the NPL for the next measurement period.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Investment custodian statements at year-end, investment manager reports, fair value hierarchy schedule (Level 1/2/3 classification), alternative investment valuation reports (private equity, real estate fund statements), investment manager fee schedules, actual vs. expected return analysis.

title: Year-End Closing Entries - Governmental Fund (Modified Accrual)
description: Recording the year-end closing entries for a governmental fund, closing all real accounts (revenues, expenditures, other financing sources/uses) to Fund Balance.

entries.account: Other Financing Sources Control (Bond Proceeds, Transfers In)

explanation: Unlike private sector accounting where income is closed to Retained Earnings, government funds close Revenues, Expenditures, Other Financing Sources, and Other Financing Uses to FUND BALANCE. This is a standard year-end process in governmental accounting — the fund balance increases by the surplus ($1.75M in this case) or decreases by the deficit. Budget vs. actual analysis: actual revenues ($42.35M) vs. estimated revenues ($42.0M) = $350K favorable; actual expenditures ($41.25M) vs. appropriations ($39.5M) = wait, expenditures exceeded appropriations by $1.75M — this would be a compliance finding in most jurisdictions.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Government ERP systems handle closing entries automatically at year-end through a period-end close process. The budgetary entries (Estimated Revenues, Appropriations, Encumbrances) are also closed separately as part of the year-end process. Finance staff must run the closing process in the correct sequence to avoid errors.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors use the closed trial balance to agree totals to the financial statements. Any revenue or expenditure recognized after the closing date requires a reopening of the books — post-closing adjustments are a risk area. The final fund balance should reconcile to the statement of revenues, expenditures, and changes in fund balance ending balance.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Trial balance before and after closing, revenue and expenditure ledger detail, closing entry documentation, reconciliation of trial balance to financial statements, post-closing trial balance, adjusting journal entries list.

title: Year-End Budgetary Closing Entries (Estimated Revenues & Appropriations)
description: Closing the budgetary control accounts (Estimated Revenues, Appropriations, and Encumbrances) at fiscal year-end — the government-specific reversal of the budget adoption entry.
explanation: The budgetary entry recorded at the start of the fiscal year (Estimated Revenues Dr, Appropriations Cr, Budgetary Fund Balance Cr/Dr) is reversed in its entirety at year-end as part of the closing process. This reversal removes the budgetary control accounts from the ledger, leaving only the GAAP accounts (revenues, expenditures, fund balance). The budgetary comparison schedule in the CAFR/ACFR uses the actual activity from the GAAP accounts compared against the adopted and final budget amounts — the comparison is made AFTER the budgetary accounts are closed.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Budgetary closing is handled separately from the GAAP closing process in government ERP systems. The sequence matters: (1) Close outstanding encumbrances (roll forward or lapse), (2) Close budgetary accounts, (3) Close GAAP accounts, (4) Run post-closing trial balance. New year budget entry is typically made at the same time as the prior year budgetary close.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors confirm that budgetary accounts are properly closed and do not carry forward balances (other than encumbrances carried by governing body action). Residual budgetary account balances after closing are a system error. The budgetary comparison schedule must reflect the final amended budget — any budget changes made after year-end that apply to the completed fiscal year require disclosure.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Budgetary close run confirmation from ERP, post-budgetary-closing trial balance (budgetary accounts at zero), outstanding encumbrance list before close, final amended budget document, new year budget entry confirmation.

title: Rate-Regulated Accounting - Regulatory Asset (Deferred Cost Recovery)
description: Deferring an operating cost that would normally be expensed immediately, because the regulator has ordered or is probable to allow recovery through future rates — creating a regulatory asset under ASC 980.

entries.account: Regulatory Asset - Deferred Storm Restoration Costs
Storm Restoration Expense (Offset - Not Charged to P&L)

explanation: This is the single most important concept in utility accounting — and the one that most surprises accountants trained in GAAP. Under ASC 980 (Rate-Regulated Enterprises), a regulated utility can defer a cost that would be expensed immediately under normal GAAP if (1) it is probable the cost will be included in future rates, and (2) future revenues will be provided to recover these costs. Instead of hitting the income statement, the cost becomes a Regulatory Asset on the balance sheet. The asset is amortized into expense over the recovery period authorized by the Public Utility Commission (PUC). Without this framework, utilities would show extreme income volatility from one-time events that regulators have guaranteed to recover.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Utility ERP systems (SAP IS-U, Oracle Utilities, Ventyx) must maintain a regulatory asset sub-ledger tracking each deferred cost, the regulatory authorization, the recovery period, and the amortization schedule. The FERC Uniform System of Accounts (for electric utilities) specifies account numbers for regulatory assets (Account 182.3 Other Regulatory Assets). Each regulatory asset requires a specific regulatory order or commission precedent supporting its deferral.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors assess the probability of regulatory recovery for every regulatory asset on the balance sheet. This is a critical going concern consideration — if a utility undergoes deregulation or loses a rate case, regulatory assets must be immediately written off, which can exceed net income many times over. Auditors review rate case orders, commission proceedings, and legal counsel opinions on recovery probability. The aggregate regulatory asset balance is typically one of the largest items on a regulated utility's balance sheet.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Regulatory order authorizing the deferral (or management's documented assessment that recovery is probable based on prior orders/precedent), cost documentation supporting the deferred amount, recovery period determination from rate case or commission order, amortization schedule, disclosure in financial statement notes of each material regulatory asset.

title: Regulatory Asset - Amortization Over Authorized Recovery Period
description: Recording the systematic amortization of a regulatory asset into expense as recovery is achieved through customer rates, over the period authorized by the public utility commission.

entries.account: Storm Restoration Expense (Now Flowing to P&L)
Regulatory Asset - Deferred Storm Restoration Costs

explanation: Once the PUC authorizes recovery of a deferred cost over a specified period (e.g., 10 years), the regulatory asset is amortized into expense at the authorized rate ($48.5M / 10 years = $4.85M/year). Simultaneously, the utility is collecting these costs from customers through rates — the revenue from customers covers the amortization expense, resulting in net zero income impact. This symmetry is the entire logic of rate-regulated accounting: costs are matched to the revenues that recover them.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Configure amortization schedules in the regulatory asset sub-ledger linked to the specific rate case order authorizing recovery. If the PUC subsequently changes the recovery period (e.g., accelerates or extends), the amortization schedule must be updated prospectively. Track the regulatory asset balance against the authorized recovery schedule to identify any over/under-recovery positions.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the amortization rate matches the PUC-authorized recovery period. Accelerating amortization beyond the authorized rate may be improper (over-expensing); slowing it below the authorized rate understates expense. If the utility is under-collecting from customers (rates not yet updated), the revenue match may not exist — assess continued deferral appropriateness.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: PUC order specifying recovery period and amortization methodology, amortization schedule reconciling to the order, rate case tariff showing the recovery rider included in customer rates, FERC Form 1 or state regulatory financial report showing the balance.

title: Regulatory Liability - Over-Collection from Customers (Refund Obligation)
description: Recording a regulatory liability when the utility has collected more from customers than its authorized revenue requirement, creating an obligation to refund or credit customers in future periods.
explanation: Regulatory liabilities arise when the utility has collected amounts from customers that it is obligated to refund (the mirror image of regulatory assets). Common causes: (1) Fuel cost adjustment over-collection (fuel costs fell but rates had not yet been adjusted down); (2) Tax reform savings not yet returned to customers (the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act created massive regulatory liabilities when corporate tax rates fell from 35% to 21%); (3) Rate case refund ordered when interim rates exceed final authorized rates. Regulatory liabilities are NOT ordinary liabilities — they represent obligations to reduce future rates.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track regulatory liabilities by type and regulatory docket in the sub-ledger. The TCJA-related regulatory liability (excess deferred income taxes — EDIT) became one of the largest regulatory liabilities ever created, as regulators required utilities to return accumulated deferred taxes at the old 35% rate that were now only needed at 21%. EDIT amortization periods are set by the IRS normalization rules — violating these rules can cause loss of accelerated depreciation.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify regulatory liabilities represent genuine obligations to refund or reduce future rates, not just management's preference to defer revenue. The specific regulatory order or settlement must be identified for each liability. TCJA-related EDIT amortization must comply with IRS normalization rules — an area of significant auditor scrutiny since 2018.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: PUC order or settlement creating the refund obligation, calculation of over-collection amount, refund methodology (rate reduction, bill credit, or rider), regulatory liability amortization schedule, TCJA normalization compliance memo for EDIT regulatory liabilities.

title: Regulatory Disallowance - Write-Off of Regulatory Asset Denied by Regulator
description: Writing off a regulatory asset when the public utility commission denies recovery, ruling that the costs are imprudent, excessive, or not in the public interest — a potentially catastrophic earnings event.
explanation: A regulatory disallowance occurs when the PUC rules that a deferred cost (or a portion of plant in service) will NOT be recovered through future rates. The entire denied amount is immediately written off to expense — it cannot be recovered and has no future economic value. Historical examples: nuclear power plant construction cost disallowances (1980s-1990s, multi-billion dollar write-offs), coal plant early retirement disallowances. This is typically the largest single-year earnings hit a regulated utility can face and is often disclosed as a special charge. Under ASC 980-360-35, if it becomes probable that part of the cost will be disallowed, impairment is required.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: A disallowance may be announced in a draft PUC order before the final order is issued. Under ASC 980, if disallowance becomes probable before the final order, the write-off must be recognized immediately — not when the order is final. This requires continuous monitoring of regulatory proceedings. Partial disallowances (only a portion denied) create complex accounting for the allowed and disallowed portions.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Regulatory disallowances are audit-critical events. Auditors monitor regulatory proceedings for all utilities in their portfolio and assess the probability of disallowance at each reporting date. A probable disallowance that is not recognized is a material overstatement of assets. Legal counsel opinions and expert testimony in the rate case are key evidence. Auditors examine the legal docket closely as cases approach decision.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: PUC draft and final orders, rate case testimony, management's probability assessment memo, legal counsel opinion, impairment calculation, board disclosure of the disallowance, financial statement restatement analysis (if recognized early vs. final order).

title: Rate Case Filing Costs - Deferred as Regulatory Asset
description: Capitalizing the legal, consulting, and expert witness costs of filing a general rate case as a regulatory asset, amortized over the rate case period upon PUC approval of the new rates.

entries.account: Rate Case Legal & Consulting Costs (Deferred from P&L)

explanation: Rate cases (formal proceedings before the PUC to set new utility rates) involve massive expenditures: regulatory attorneys ($500K–$2M), expert witnesses (cost of service consultants, economists, engineers), commission staff interactions, and hearing preparation. These costs are incurred to obtain authorization for future revenues. Under ASC 980, these costs are deferred as a regulatory asset if it is probable that the rate case will result in new rates and these costs will be recovered. Upon approval of new rates, the deferral is amortized over the rate case period (typically 3–5 years until the next rate case).

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track rate case costs by vendor and category in a project code. The deferral decision requires ongoing assessment of the probability of rate case success. If the rate case is withdrawn or denied without new rates, the deferred costs are immediately written off. Upon rate approval, begin amortization over the new rate period.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors assess the probability of cost recovery — particularly in contested cases where intervenors are challenging cost levels. Costs of lost rate cases should not be deferred. The amortization period must align with the regulatory-approved rate period, not management's preference.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Rate case filing documents, invoices from legal counsel and consultants, PUC docket number and proceeding status, probability of approval assessment, PUC order approving rates (for amortization commencement), amortization schedule.

title: Pension / OPEB Regulatory Asset - Deferred Under ASC 980 vs. ASC 715
description: Recording the portion of unrecognized pension and OPEB costs (that would be charged to OCI under ASC 715) as a regulatory asset instead, because the PUC allows recovery of pension costs through future rates.

entries.account: Regulatory Asset - Deferred Pension & OPEB Costs (ASC 980)

explanation: This is a uniquely regulated utility accounting concept. Under ASC 715, unrecognized actuarial losses and prior service costs flow through OCI (reducing equity). However, for regulated utilities, these costs will be recovered through future rates — therefore, deferring to OCI understates the utility's future earnings from rate recovery. Under ASC 980, regulated utilities record these costs as Regulatory Assets instead of OCI. This means a regulated utility can have a much higher equity than an unregulated company facing identical pension obligations, because the rate recovery is a real asset. This is an area of significant financial statement analysis attention.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The actuarial valuation determines the OCI component that would normally be recorded. For the portion allocable to regulated operations, redirect the OCI entry to the Regulatory Asset account. Non-regulated subsidiaries of the same holding company must use normal ASC 715 OCI treatment. The bifurcation between regulated and unregulated operations requires careful tracking.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that only the regulated portion of pension costs is deferred to a regulatory asset. If the utility has non-regulated subsidiaries or non-regulated operations, the appropriate cost allocation must be documented. PUC approval for pension cost recovery in rates must be demonstrated — not all regulators automatically allow deferred pension cost recovery.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Actuarial valuation report with OCI component, PUC orders allowing pension cost recovery in rates, regulatory vs. non-regulatory cost allocation methodology, regulatory asset roll-forward, pension cost amortization schedule used in rate cases.

title: Stranded Cost Regulatory Asset - Deregulation Transition Costs
description: Recording stranded costs as a regulatory asset when a utility transitions from regulated monopoly to competitive markets, representing assets and costs that are no longer recoverable through market prices.

entries.account: Plant in Service - Uneconomic Generation Assets (Reclassed)

explanation: When electric utility markets deregulate (as occurred in California, Texas, PJM, and New England in the 1990s-2000s), generation assets built under regulated cost-of-service pricing may be 'stranded' — worth less in competitive markets than their book value. Regulators established transition charges (competitive transition assessments / CTAs) that allowed utilities to recover stranded costs from customers over a transition period. The stranded assets are reclassified from Plant in Service to Regulatory Assets, amortized as the transition charges flow in. If recovery is not authorized, an immediate write-down to fair value is required.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Stranded cost accounting required complete restructuring of the utility's balance sheet in deregulating states. The regulatory asset replaces the plant on the balance sheet. Track separately: generation asset stranded costs, above-market PPA costs, and regulatory transition costs. Amortize based on the authorized CTA collection period.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The probability of stranded cost recovery must be assessed each period. If competitive market prices fall further below the regulatory asset's carrying value (meaning more stranded cost than authorized for recovery), additional write-down may be required. Auditors in deregulating states focus heavily on the adequacy of stranded cost regulatory asset reserves.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Deregulation statute and regulatory order authorizing stranded cost recovery, stranded cost calculation (market value vs. book value by asset), CTA tariff and collection schedule, amortization schedule, ongoing assessment of market prices vs. authorized recovery levels.

title: Revenue Decoupling Mechanism - Adjustment for Sales Volume Variance
description: Recording the decoupling adjustment to revenue where the utility's authorized revenue requirement is independent of actual sales volumes, preventing utility earnings from varying with conservation.
explanation: Decoupling breaks the traditional link between utility profits and sales volumes — addressing the 'throughput incentive' problem where utilities have no financial incentive to promote conservation (more sales = more profit). Under decoupling, the regulator sets an authorized revenue level. If actual sales are below the authorized level (because customers conserved), the utility records a regulatory asset (under-collection) and will collect the difference through a future rate surcharge. If sales are above authorized (customers used more), a regulatory liability is created. California pioneered electric decoupling in the 1970s.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The decoupling calculation compares authorized revenue per customer (by class) to actual revenue per customer, multiplied by actual customer count. The variance is accumulated monthly and recovered/refunded in the following year's rates. Maintain the decoupling mechanism balance by customer class (residential, commercial, industrial) as regulators often require separate tracking.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors assess the probability of decoupling mechanism recovery, which is typically very high (it is a regulatory obligation, not a management estimate). The calculation methodology should be verified against the tariff provisions. Large decoupling mechanism balances can arise during periods of rapid energy efficiency improvement or mild weather.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: PUC order authorizing the decoupling mechanism, decoupling tariff provisions, monthly calculation of authorized vs. actual revenue by customer class, decoupling mechanism balance roll-forward, rate schedule showing future collection/refund mechanism.

title: Utility Acquisition Premium - Regulatory Asset for Goodwill Recovery
description: Recording the acquisition premium paid above book value for a regulated utility as a regulatory asset when the PUC has authorized its recovery through future rates, rather than immediate write-off to goodwill.

entries.account: Goodwill (GAAP - Remeasured Where Regulatory Recovery Authorized)

explanation: When one regulated utility acquires another, the purchase price typically exceeds book value, creating goodwill under ASC 805. However, unlike commercial goodwill (not amortized, tested for impairment), regulated utility goodwill may be reclassified as a Regulatory Asset if the PUC authorizes recovery through future customer rates. The distinction matters enormously: commercial goodwill is impairment-tested (mark-to-market risk); regulatory goodwill is amortized over the authorized recovery period (predictable, rate-guaranteed). This is a merger condition negotiated with regulators as part of merger approval proceedings.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The PUC's merger approval order will specify: (1) whether acquisition premium recovery is authorized, (2) the amortization period, and (3) any consumer benefits (rate credits, rate freezes) required as quid pro quo for premium recovery. Track the regulatory asset separately from commercial goodwill in the balance sheet. FERC may separately approve or deny acquisition premium recovery for jurisdictional assets.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that the specific PUC order authorizes acquisition premium recovery — not just that merger was approved. Regulatory approval of a merger does not automatically authorize acquisition premium recovery. The amortization period must be clearly specified. Impairment testing of the regulatory asset (for continued probability of recovery) differs from ASC 350 goodwill testing.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: PUC merger approval order specifying acquisition premium recovery terms, amortization schedule per the order, rate case testimony supporting the premium, FERC authorization (for FERC-jurisdictional utilities), consumer benefit commitments and compliance tracking.

title: Retail Electric Revenue - Cycle Billing to Residential & Commercial Customers
description: Recording monthly retail electricity revenue from meter readings, segmented by customer class (residential, commercial, industrial) with demand charges and energy charges billed separately.
explanation: Utility revenue is recognized when electricity is delivered to customers (over time — the delivery is the performance obligation under ASC 606). The tariff structure differs by class: residential customers pay a flat rate per kWh (energy charge only); commercial customers pay energy charges plus a demand charge (based on peak kW usage within the billing period); industrial customers pay complex multi-part tariffs with energy, demand, transmission, and distribution components. Under ASC 606, utilities recognize revenue as electricity flows to the customer — not when invoiced.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Utility billing systems (SAP IS-U, Oracle Utilities, Itron) read meters, calculate charges based on tariffs, and generate bills. The bill generation cycle is staggered throughout the month (different meters read on different days). Integration between the billing system and the general ledger automates revenue recognition. Tariff accuracy is critical — errors in rate codes cause systematic revenue over/under-billing.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Revenue is the highest-risk area for utility auditors. Key procedures: (1) Test tariff rates billed vs. PUC-approved tariff schedules, (2) Reconcile total kWh billed to the system's metered output (accounting for line losses), (3) Test controls over meter reading (meter tampering, meter reading errors), (4) Verify unbilled revenue accrual methodology, (5) Assess adequacy of bad debt allowance by customer class.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: PUC-approved tariff schedules by customer class, meter reading records, billing system reports by customer class, kWh billed reconciliation to metered generation/purchases, accounts receivable aging by class, bad debt write-off history.

title: Unbilled Revenue Accrual - Electricity Delivered But Not Yet Billed (Cycle Billing)
description: Accruing revenue for electricity delivered between the last meter reading date and fiscal period-end, representing usage that has occurred but will not be billed until the next meter reading cycle.
explanation: Because meters are read on a staggered cycle (different customers read on different days throughout the month), a portion of delivered electricity at month-end has not yet been billed. This 'unbilled revenue' is a significant accrual — for a large electric utility, it can represent 10%–20% of monthly revenue. The accrual is estimated using: average days of unbilled service per customer class × average daily revenue rate. Upon next billing, the unbilled receivable is reversed and replaced with a billed receivable. This is a recurring entry that reverses and re-accrues each period.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Most utility billing systems calculate the unbilled accrual automatically based on meter read dates, tariff rates, and estimated usage patterns for the unbilled period. The estimate uses actual degree-days and customer count for weather-sensitive residential loads. The unbilled accrual is one of the largest estimates on a utility's balance sheet — changes in the methodology can have material income impacts.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test the unbilled revenue accrual by: (1) Comparing the accrual methodology to prior periods for consistency, (2) Testing the degree-day and usage assumptions against weather data, (3) Tracing the subsequent month's billing to verify the accrual was reasonable, (4) Reconciling unbilled estimates to actual billing in the following period. The unbilled reversal/re-accrual cycle must be documented.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Billing system unbilled accrual calculation report, average daily usage by customer class, degree-day data from weather service, customer count by class and meter read date, subsequent period billing vs. prior accrual reconciliation, methodology documentation.

title: Fuel Cost Adjustment (FCA) / Fuel Adjustment Clause - Over-Collection Regulatory Liability
description: Recording the over-collection of fuel costs from customers through the Fuel Cost Adjustment (FCA) rider when actual fuel costs were lower than the forecast embedded in current rates, creating a regulatory liability.
explanation: Most regulated utilities have a Fuel Cost Adjustment (FCA) or Energy Cost Adjustment (ECA) clause that allows periodic (monthly, quarterly, or annual) adjustment of rates to reflect actual fuel cost changes without a full rate case. The clause includes a 'true-up' mechanism: if actual fuel costs are lower than the forecast used to set the FCA rate, the over-collection is tracked as a regulatory liability and refunded to customers in the next adjustment period. This prevents utilities from profiting from favorable fuel cost variances — regulators pass all fuel savings and costs directly to customers.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track FCA collections separately from base rate revenue. The FCA regulatory liability or asset is the running balance between actual fuel costs incurred and amounts collected through the FCA rider. Many utilities calculate this balance monthly and report it to the PUC in monthly FCA compliance filings. The balance is carried on the balance sheet until cleared through rate adjustments.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the FCA mechanism calculation against the tariff provisions and PUC orders. The fuel cost basis (what costs are includable in the FCA — typically natural gas at spot or contract prices, purchased power, coal, nuclear fuel) must match the tariff definition exactly. Costs outside the defined fuel categories must not be included in the FCA.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: FCA tariff clause and PUC order defining fuel costs eligible for tracking, monthly FCA balance calculation, actual fuel costs by fuel type, FCA rate history, PUC compliance filings, over/under-collection balance reconciliation.

title: Fuel Cost Adjustment - Under-Collection Regulatory Asset (Fuel Costs Exceeded Forecast)
description: Recording a regulatory asset when actual fuel costs exceed the amounts collected from customers through the Fuel Cost Adjustment rider, creating a deferred cost to be recovered through future rate increases.

entries.account: Regulatory Asset - FCA Under-Collection (Deferred Fuel Costs)
Fuel Expense (Deferred from P&L — To Be Recovered)

explanation: The mirror image of over-collection: when natural gas prices spike, fuel costs exceed the forecast embedded in current FCA rates. The difference is deferred as a regulatory asset (the utility is owed this from customers through future rate increases). Classic example: the February 2021 Texas winter storm caused catastrophic natural gas price spikes — utilities that operated through this event had massive FCA under-collections (billions in some cases). These are recoverable from customers through rate adjustments, but the recovery period can be extended over years to avoid rate shock.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Large, sudden FCA under-collections (like storm events) may require emergency rate applications to accelerate recovery. The carrying costs (interest) on the unrecovered FCA balance may also be recoverable through a carrying charge included in the FCA tariff. Track carrying charge accruals as additional regulatory assets.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: During periods of extreme fuel price spikes, auditors assess whether the FCA under-collection is fully recoverable — particularly if the utility was subject to force majeure events that might limit customer obligations. The interest/carrying charge rate on the FCA balance must be within the tariff-authorized rate.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: FCA tariff with authorized carrying charge rate, monthly fuel cost tracking vs. FCA collections, FCA balance with carrying charge accrual, PUC emergency rate application (if filed), customer notification of FCA balance and recovery plan.

title: Wholesale Power Sales - FERC-Regulated Market Revenue
description: Recording revenue from wholesale electricity sales in organized wholesale markets (PJM, MISO, CAISO, SPP) at market clearing prices, recognized at the time of delivery.
explanation: Utilities that sell power into organized wholesale markets (Regional Transmission Organizations like PJM, MISO, CAISO) recognize revenue at the real-time or day-ahead Locational Marginal Price (LMP) as power is delivered. Wholesale revenue is subject to FERC (not state PUC) jurisdiction. Large utilities may simultaneously be buyers and sellers in wholesale markets — netting is not permitted absent regulatory guidance. FERC market settlements (daily or monthly) drive the billing process. Revenue is highly volatile, tied to LMP which can swing from negative to thousands of dollars per MWh.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: RTO/ISO settlement statements (from PJM, MISO, etc.) are received monthly and represent the authoritative source for wholesale market revenues and costs. These statements are complex — they include real-time energy, day-ahead energy, capacity, ancillary services, and transmission congestion components. The settlement statement must be reconciled to the utility's own meter data and position management system.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify wholesale revenue against RTO/ISO settlement statements. Reconciling the utility's internal generation records (MW dispatched by hour) to the RTO settlement statement tests completeness and accuracy. Significant unreconciled differences may indicate metering errors or settlement disputes.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: RTO/ISO settlement statements by market interval, meter data management system records (MWh by generating unit by hour), price verification (LMP by node and interval), disputes log for settlement discrepancies, FERC Form 1 wholesale revenue reporting.

title: Capacity Market Revenue - Forward Capacity Auction Obligation
description: Recording revenue from capacity market auction commitments (PJM RPM, ISO-NE FCM) where the utility receives fixed capacity payments in exchange for committing generation capacity to be available during peak demand periods.
explanation: Capacity markets compensate generators not for energy produced, but for being available. In PJM's Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) and ISO-NE's Forward Capacity Market (FCM), generators bid into auctions years in advance, committing to be available during the delivery year. The capacity price ($/MW-Day) is set at the clearing price. Revenue is recognized ratably over the commitment period as the availability obligation is met. Non-performance during scarcity hours results in capacity market penalties that reduce net revenue.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Capacity revenue is recognized over the performance period (typically a one-year delivery period that begins 3 years after the auction). Track capacity commitments by generating unit and delivery year in the capacity position management system. Performance penalties (for failure to perform during called hours) must be accrued as they become probable.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify capacity market settlements against RTO auction clearing prices and committed MW. Performance penalties are a significant audit area — failure to accurately accrue penalties overstates capacity revenue. New units that fail to achieve commercial operation before the delivery year start must assess the impact on their capacity obligations.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: RTO capacity auction clearing results (MW and $/MW-Day cleared), capacity commitment agreements, monthly capacity settlement statements from RTO, performance data during high-demand periods, penalty calculation documentation, capacity position by unit and delivery year.

title: Ancillary Services Revenue - Frequency Regulation, Spinning Reserve
description: Recording revenue from providing ancillary services (frequency regulation, spinning reserve, operating reserve) to the transmission system operator, recognized as the service availability obligation is fulfilled.
explanation: Beyond energy and capacity, generators can earn ancillary service revenue by providing grid reliability services: (1) Frequency Regulation: rapidly adjusting output to maintain grid frequency at 60 Hz — paid a capability payment plus a performance payment; (2) Spinning Reserve: maintaining generation online and ready to ramp up within 10 minutes; (3) Non-Spinning Reserve: able to commit within 30 minutes.
