If deductions are made from the retention for unremedied defects, recognize the deducted amount as Other Income (recovery of remediation cost).
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check that retention releases are authorized by the project engineer and supported by a Defects Completion Certificate. Releasing retention without proper authorization (or before the DLP has expired) is a control failure. Significant deductions from retention suggest either poor construction quality or disputes with the contractor — both may have implications for the CIP asset's carrying value.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Defects Completion Certificate from the project engineer, retention release authorization, bank transfer confirmation, Retention Payable sub-ledger cleared to zero, any deductions from retention (with supporting evidence of the defect and cost of repair), and project close-out report.

title: How to Transfer a Completed Building from Construction in Progress to a Depreciable Fixed Asset
description: Reclassifying the accumulated CIP balance to a Building fixed asset when the occupancy certificate is received and depreciation begins.
explanation: This critical transfer entry is made when the building receives its occupancy certificate. Depreciation begins from this date, not from when construction started.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Transfer from CIP to the Building fixed asset account on the date the asset is available for its intended use — typically when the occupancy certificate (or equivalent from the municipality) is issued. This is also when: (a) IAS 23 borrowing cost capitalization ceases, (b) depreciation commences, and (c) the asset becomes subject to IAS 36 impairment testing (rather than the simpler CIP impairment assessment). Ensure all related costs (professional fees, permits, retention) are fully accrued before the transfer.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The transfer date determines when depreciation starts — auditors confirm this matches the occupancy certificate date. Delaying the transfer (keeping the building in CIP after it is available for use) defers depreciation and overstates CIP. Any costs incurred after the transfer date (routine maintenance, operating costs) must be expensed rather than capitalized. The useful life determination at the point of transfer drives all future depreciation charges.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Occupancy certificate from the municipality (confirming the building is approved for use), CIP roll-forward showing the full accumulated cost, Building fixed asset register entry (cost, useful life, depreciation method, start date), IAS 23 capitalization cessation confirmation, depreciation schedule from the transfer date, and IAS 36 impairment assessment for the newly recognized fixed asset.

title: How to Record an Approved Construction Change Order That Increases Project Scope and Cost
description: Capitalizing additional costs from a developer-approved variation order issued to the main contractor.
explanation: Approved change orders increase the total construction cost. They are capitalized into CIP and increase the eventual cost of the completed building.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Record only approved (signed) change orders — do not capitalize unapproved variation claims or contractor requests that have not been formally agreed. Maintain a change order register tracking: change order number, description, cost, approval date, and CIP impact. Update the project budget for each approved change order. Accumulating too many change orders may indicate inadequate initial scope definition or scope creep — both signals that management should investigate the project's viability.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify change orders are genuinely approved (signed by both developer and contractor) and relate to real scope changes (not contractor claims for additional cost without legitimate grounds). Unauthorized change orders that increase CIP without board approval where the amounts are material are a governance failure. Change orders that are in fact correcting contractor defects (rectification work) should not be capitalized — they should be recovered from the contractor or charged against the retention.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Signed change order form (developer and contractor signatures), change order register, updated project budget showing the scope and cost change, quantity surveyor's assessment of the additional work value, approval authority sign-off (board or investment committee if above threshold), and contractor invoice referencing the change order number.

title: How to Record Liquidated Damages Recovered from a Contractor for Late Project Delivery
description: Deducting a delay penalty from the contractor's payment and recognizing it as other income.
explanation: Liquidated damages recovered from a contractor for late delivery reduce the amount owed to them. They are recorded as other income because they offset the financial loss from delays.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Liquidated damages (LDs) are a pre-agreed daily or weekly penalty for contractor delay, specified in the contract. Deduct from the contractor's payment when invoiced — do not offset against the CIP asset cost (LDs are a separate commercial remedy, not a reduction in the value of work done). Recognize as Other Income in the period the LD deduction is made. Note: some developers are reluctant to apply LDs for fear of damaging the contractor relationship — this is a commercial decision, but if LDs are contractually due, failure to enforce may constitute a breach of fiduciary duty to shareholders.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check that LDs are assessed correctly per the contract (daily rate × days of delay, from the contractual completion date to actual completion, subject to any employer-caused extensions of time). If LDs are due but not applied, auditors may question whether this represents a commercial concession with value that should be disclosed. LDs are taxable income in the period they are recognized.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Construction contract (LD rate, definition of delay, contractor's notice of completion), project completion date vs. contractual completion date, LD calculation (days × daily rate), LD deduction from contractor payment certificate, contractor's objection or acceptance of the LD deduction, and Other Income ledger entry.

title: How to Capitalize a Mandatory Infrastructure Contribution Paid to the Municipality as a CIP Cost
description: Adding a compulsory municipality infrastructure levy (road access, utilities connection) to the construction project cost.
explanation: Mandatory government contributions required to develop a plot (road access, utilities connection) are directly attributable to the project and must be capitalized into CIP.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Infrastructure contributions paid to the municipality as conditions of the building permit (road construction, sewage connection, water supply connection, streetlighting) are directly attributable to bringing the development to its intended use — capitalize to CIP. The contribution will form part of the completed building's total cost when transferred from CIP. Voluntary CSR contributions to the municipality beyond the permit requirements are expensed.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that infrastructure contributions are legally mandatory (specified in the permit conditions) rather than voluntary. Mandatory contributions have a clear official receipt from the municipality. Payments to individuals or intermediaries rather than directly to the municipality are red flags for anti-bribery concerns. For investment properties, infrastructure contributions form part of the initial cost under IAS 40.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Building permit conditions specifying the infrastructure contribution requirement, municipality official receipt for the contribution, nature of the infrastructure work funded, CIP allocation, direct payment to municipality (not via intermediary), and project budget showing infrastructure contribution allowance.

title: How to Initially Recognize an Investment Property at Cost Under IAS 40
description: Recording a building purchased specifically to generate rental income as an investment property using the cost model.
explanation: Under IAS 40, a property held to earn rental income or for capital appreciation is classified as Investment Property. It can be measured at cost or fair value.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Investment property is initially measured at cost — including purchase price, transfer taxes, legal fees, and other directly attributable acquisition costs. After initial recognition, choose either the cost model (depreciate the building, test for impairment) or the fair value model (no depreciation, annual fair value revaluation to P&L). Once the fair value model is elected, it must be applied to all investment properties consistently. The choice of model significantly affects reported profit — the fair value model is more common for listed real estate companies.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the classification as investment property (not PPE) — the key test is whether the property is held to earn rental income or for capital appreciation, rather than for use in operations. Mixed-use properties (partially owner-occupied, partially rental) require splitting — the rental portion is investment property, the owner-occupied portion is PPE. The cost model requires annual depreciation and IAS 36 impairment testing.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sale and purchase agreement, transfer tax receipt, acquisition cost schedule (all directly attributable costs), IAS 40 classification assessment (rental income vs. own use), accounting policy election (cost model vs. fair value model), investment property register entry, depreciation schedule (cost model) or fair value assessment calendar (fair value model), and tenant rental agreement confirming rental intent.

title: How to Record an Annual Investment Property Fair Value Gain Under IAS 40
description: Adjusting an investment property's carrying value upward following an independent annual valuation, with the gain recognized in profit or loss.
explanation: Under the IAS 40 Fair Value model, any increase in a property's market value goes directly to the income statement — unlike PPE revaluation which goes to OCI. The property is not depreciated.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Obtain an independent RICS-qualified valuation at each annual reporting date. The fair value gain or loss goes directly to P&L — this is a critical distinction from IAS 16 PPE revaluation (which goes to OCI). Under the fair value model, no depreciation is charged on the investment property. The annual fair value movement is the primary driver of profit/loss variability for real estate investment companies. Maintain a fair value movement schedule per property.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: See revaluation-investment-property-gain for audit considerations. Additional note: the IAS 40 fair value model produces P&L volatility that may not reflect underlying economic performance — companies often disclose EPRA (European Public Real Estate Association) metrics to provide an alternative view of performance excluding fair value movements.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Independent RICS-qualified valuation report, valuation methodology (income capitalization rate, comparable sales, DCF), comparison to prior year valuation, fair value movement schedule, income statement presentation (gain shown separately), deferred tax on the gain, and investment property note disclosure including fair value movement reconciliation.

title: How to Record an Annual Investment Property Fair Value Loss When Market Values Decline
description: Reducing an investment property's carrying value following a downward independent valuation, with the loss recognized in profit or loss.
explanation: Under IAS 40, decreases in fair value also go directly to the income statement. This can significantly impact reported profits in a falling market.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Under the IAS 40 fair value model, losses are recognized symmetrically with gains — both go directly to P&L. Unlike IAS 16 PPE revaluation (where a loss only goes to P&L to the extent it exceeds the revaluation surplus), there is no OCI component for investment property fair value losses. The loss can create a deferred tax benefit (DTA) if the tax base of the property exceeds its new carrying value.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors scrutinize fair value losses less than fair value gains — companies may be reluctant to recognize losses promptly. A property with declining market rents, increasing vacancy, or locational factors suggesting value deterioration should show a fair value loss. If the independent valuer shows a decline but management rejects the valuation as too pessimistic without objective grounds, auditors may require an additional independent opinion.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Independent valuer's report supporting the reduction in fair value, comparison to prior year valuation with explanation of market factors causing the decline, income statement presentation of the loss (separately disclosed), deferred tax benefit calculation on the loss, investment property note disclosure, and management's assessment of the valuation approach and assumptions.

title: How to Transfer an Owner-Occupied Property to Investment Property When the Company Begins Leasing It Out
description: Reclassifying a company-used building to investment property when it is leased to a third party, with the gain going to OCI.
explanation: When transferring from PPE to Investment Property at fair value, the gain is initially recognized in OCI — consistent with PPE revaluation rules, not in P&L.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The trigger for transfer is the commencement of an operating lease to a third party. At the transfer date: (1) derecognize the PPE cost and accumulated depreciation, (2) recognize the investment property at fair value, and (3) credit the difference between fair value and net book value to OCI (Revaluation Surplus) — not P&L. This is because the IAS 16 revaluation model applies at the point of transfer from PPE. Once classified as investment property, subsequent fair value changes go to P&L (if the fair value model is adopted).
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that the transfer is supported by an actual lease agreement (not just an intention to let). The fair value at the transfer date requires an independent professional valuation. The gain goes to OCI — any proposal to take the gain to P&L at transfer is incorrect. The Revaluation Surplus in OCI is not subsequently reclassified to P&L (unlike cash flow hedges) — it stays in OCI and is transferred directly to retained earnings when the property is sold.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement confirming the commencement of letting to a third party, independent fair value valuation at transfer date, IAS 40 transfer entry (PPE → Investment Property), OCI Revaluation Surplus calculation, accumulated depreciation derecognition, subsequent fair value model application, and IAS 12 deferred tax on the OCI gain.

title: How to Transfer Investment Property to Inventory When the Developer Decides to Sell
description: Moving a building from investment property to inventory at its current carrying value when the intention changes from hold to sell.
explanation: When the intention changes from holding to selling, the property transfers to inventory at its current carrying value. No gain or loss is recorded at the transfer date.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The transfer from Investment Property to Inventory (IAS 2) is at the current carrying value — no gain or loss at transfer. If the investment property was measured at fair value under IAS 40, the inventory is initially recorded at that fair value. Once in inventory, the property is measured at the lower of cost (which is the fair value at transfer) or NRV under IAS 2. This transfer is triggered by commencement of active development for sale (not just a management decision to sell someday).
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that the transfer is triggered by a genuine change of use (active development for sale), not merely a commercial decision to sell an existing investment property. If the property is actively marketed for sale without development, it should remain as investment property (sold as investment property, not inventory). The cost basis for COGS calculation is the fair value at the transfer date — this affects the gross margin on eventual sale.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Management decision or board approval to sell the property (with development plan if applicable), evidence of active development commencing (contractor appointment, permits, design work), transfer entry at current carrying value, IAS 2 inventory register entry (with cost = fair value at transfer), IAS 2 NRV assessment at each subsequent reporting date, and COGS basis documentation for eventual sale.

title: How to Record a Gain on the Disposal of Investment Property
description: Removing an investment property from the books and recognizing the gain when it sells above its carrying value.

entries.account: Gain on Disposal of Investment Property

explanation: Gains on disposal of investment property go to the income statement. The asset is removed at its last revalued carrying amount.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Derecognize the investment property at its last carrying value (the most recent fair value if the fair value model was used, or the depreciated cost if the cost model was used). The gain = Sale proceeds minus Carrying value minus Transaction costs (broker fees, legal fees, transfer taxes on the disposal). Present the gain as a separate line in the income statement — investors and analysts separately assess operating rental income from property trading gains.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Revenue recognition timing: recognize on the date title transfers to the buyer and the developer has no remaining obligations — typically the date of registration at the Lands & Survey Department in Jordan. If the sale is conditional (subject to planning consent, tenant vacating), revenue should be deferred until conditions are met. Broker fees and legal costs paid by the seller are deducted from the gain — ensure they are not expensed separately and recognized again as a cost.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sale and purchase agreement, title transfer documentation (Lands & Survey Department registration), sale proceeds bank receipt, investment property derecognition at carrying value, gain calculation (proceeds minus carrying value minus transaction costs), broker commission and legal fee invoices, income tax calculation on the gain, and investment property register update.

title: How to Record a Loss on the Disposal of Investment Property When Sold Below Carrying Value
description: Derecognizing an investment property and recording the loss when sale proceeds are less than the carrying value.

entries.account: Loss on Disposal of Investment Property

explanation: If the property sells below its carrying value, the difference is an immediate loss on the income statement.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: For properties using the fair value model, a sale below the most recent fair value suggests either the independent valuation was too high or market conditions deteriorated between the valuation date and sale date. For properties using the cost model, the loss is the net book value minus proceeds. Transaction costs (paid by the seller) further reduce the proceeds — the net loss is slightly higher than the gross price gap. Present disposal losses separately from operating rental income for clear financial reporting.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Disposal losses on investment properties that were held at fair value under IAS 40 are unusual — if the fair value model is correctly applied with up-to-date professional valuations, the carrying value should approximate what the market will pay. A significant disposal loss shortly after the last fair value revaluation suggests the prior year fair value was overstated — potentially requiring a prior period restatement assessment.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sale and purchase agreement, title transfer documentation, sale proceeds bank receipt, investment property derecognition at carrying value, loss calculation, most recent fair value valuation (for comparison), transaction cost invoices, IAS 36 or IAS 40 prior period assessment (if loss is significantly below last fair value), and income tax treatment of the loss.

title: How to Record an Off-Plan Unit Booking Deposit as Deferred Revenue Before Construction Begins
description: Treating a buyer's off-plan deposit as a liability because the performance obligation has not yet been fulfilled.
explanation: Cash collected before the building is complete is a liability. Under IFRS 15, revenue is only recognized when control of the unit passes to the buyer — typically at handover.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Under IFRS 15, revenue recognition for off-plan sales requires a careful assessment: does control transfer over time (percentage of completion) or at a point in time (handover)? In Jordan, off-plan sales typically transfer control at handover (the buyer cannot direct the use of the specific unit during construction, the developer retains the ability to substitute the unit), so the point-in-time model applies. All deposits and installments go to Deferred Revenue until handover. In Jordan, these funds must be held in a licensed escrow account per the Real Estate Regulatory Law.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test the IFRS 15 control transfer assessment for the specific jurisdiction and contract terms. In some jurisdictions (e.g., where the buyer's contract cannot be cancelled and they bear the residual risk of the asset), revenue may qualify for over-time recognition — each case requires individual contract analysis. The Advance from Buyers balance must reconcile to the total cash collected per buyer per unit. Escrow compliance is an additional audit area in Jordan.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Off-plan sale and purchase agreement, IFRS 15 control transfer assessment (point in time vs. over time), advance from buyers sub-ledger by unit and buyer, escrow bank account statements, Jordan Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) compliance documentation, unit delivery schedule (for timing of revenue recognition), and financial statement disclosure of aggregate advance from buyers balance.

title: How to Record Construction-Linked Instalment Collections from Off-Plan Buyers
description: Accumulating further deferred revenue as buyers make payments linked to construction milestones.
explanation: Each instalment collected adds to the deferred revenue balance. No revenue is recognized until handover. The balance sheet grows on both the asset and liability sides simultaneously.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track each instalment per buyer per unit in the Advance from Buyers sub-ledger. The per-unit deferred revenue balance grows with each collection and is released entirely at handover. For the cash flow statement, all pre-handover collections are cash inflows from operations (for property developers whose primary business is residential development) — not financing activities. Monitor the Advance from Buyers balance relative to the CIP balance — if collections significantly exceed construction costs incurred, assess whether there is a liquidity risk if buyers cancel.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors trace instalment receipts to buyer contracts and confirmed payment dates. Instalments collected in advance of the contractual payment schedule (i.e., the buyer paid before the milestone was reached) should still be deferred — recognize when the milestone occurs, not when cash arrives. The aggregate Advance from Buyers balance at year-end must reconcile to the sum of all unpaid contracted amounts not yet earned.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Instalment payment schedule per buyer per unit, bank receipt for each instalment, Advance from Buyers sub-ledger (unit-level), comparison of cash collected vs. construction cost incurred (CIP balance), escrow account statements, buyer contract confirming the instalment schedule, and deferred revenue rollforward (opening + collections − revenue recognized = closing).

title: How to Recognize Off-Plan Unit Sale Revenue at the Point of Handover Under IFRS 15
description: Releasing the full deferred revenue balance to earned revenue when the completed apartment is handed over to the buyer.
explanation: Under IFRS 15, control passes to the buyer at handover. The full deferred revenue liability is released to the income statement at that single point in time.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The handover event triggers revenue recognition — specifically the delivery of the unit keys and the signing of the handover certificate by the buyer. This is the point control passes to the buyer. Simultaneously recognize: (a) the deferred revenue release to Property Sales Revenue, and (b) the Cost of Property Sold (see re-offplan-cogs-at-handover). If the buyer refuses handover (claiming defects), revenue recognition is suspended until the dispute is resolved. Track handover completions in a unit handover register.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors trace the largest revenue transactions to signed handover certificates. Revenue recognized without a signed handover certificate is premature. They also check that the amount released from Advance from Buyers equals the total contracted price (not just the cash received if a balance is outstanding as a post-handover receivable). Year-end cut-off testing: units handed over in the last days of the year require careful examination of the handover date.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Signed handover certificate (buyer and developer signatures, date, unit details), unit completion inspection report (confirming the unit meets the contractual specifications), Advance from Buyers sub-ledger cleared to zero for the unit, Property Sales Revenue entry, cost of sales entry, post-handover receivable (if balance outstanding), and handover register.

title: How to Recognize the Cost of Sales for an Off-Plan Unit at the Point of Handover
description: Transferring the accumulated construction cost of a completed unit from CIP or inventory to Cost of Property Sold at handover.
explanation: Revenue and cost of sales must be matched. The accumulated construction cost of the unit is transferred to Cost of Property Sold at the same time as sale revenue is recognized.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: For developments with multiple units, the total CIP cost must be allocated to individual units using a reasonable method: (a) by unit size (floor area), (b) by sales price ratio, or (c) by specific identification if units are distinct. The COGS recognized at handover is the allocated unit cost — not the development average cost. Maintain a unit cost allocation schedule throughout the development. Land cost is also allocated to each unit for the COGS calculation.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the unit cost allocation methodology is reasonable and consistently applied. Using sales price as the allocation basis in a development with premium vs. standard units creates systematic cost mismatches. Auditors also check that the COGS at handover is matched to the same unit and same handover date as the revenue recognized — a unit where revenue is recognized in December but COGS is recognized in January creates a P&L mismatch.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Unit cost allocation schedule (allocation method, total CIP ÷ units, per-unit cost), CIP roll-forward showing the unit balance before transfer, cost of sales entry dated to the handover date, matching revenue recognition entry for the same unit, land cost allocation to the unit, and post-development cost reconciliation (total costs vs. total revenue for the development).

title: How to Record the Full-Cash Sale of a Ready Residential Unit with Simultaneous Revenue and COGS
description: Recording a completed unit sale paid in full, with revenue and cost of sales recognized at the point of sale.
explanation: For a ready unit sold at closing, both revenue and COGS are recognized simultaneously at the point of sale.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: For completed (ready) units sold with immediate payment, the revenue recognition trigger is the same as for off-plan handovers — title transfer and key delivery. Under Jordan's Real Estate Law, the official transfer at the Lands & Survey Department is the definitive evidence of title transfer. In the same period, recognize the unit's cost from inventory as Cost of Property Sold. The gross profit margin on ready unit sales reflects the full development economics for that unit.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Revenue recognition for ready unit sales requires evidence of title transfer — the official registry document from the Lands & Survey Department. Sales recognized based on signing of a preliminary agreement (prior to official registration) may be premature. The cost of the sold unit must match the correct unit in the inventory sub-ledger — selling Unit 5B but recognizing the cost of Unit 5A creates a COGS allocation error.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sale and purchase agreement, title transfer documentation (Lands & Survey Department registration certificate), cash receipt, unit cost identification from inventory sub-ledger, COGS entry matching the specific unit sold, gross profit reconciliation, and sales register.

title: How to Record a Completed Unit Sale Where the Buyer Uses a Bank Mortgage
description: Recognizing revenue at sale and recording a receivable from the buyer's bank when mortgage proceeds settle to the developer.
explanation: When a buyer uses a bank mortgage, the developer records a receivable from the buyer's bank. Cash arrives after the bank processes the disbursement, typically within a few days of signing.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Revenue is recognized at the point of title transfer (Lands & Survey registration) — the payment mechanism (cash or mortgage) does not affect the timing of revenue recognition. The receivable from the bank is typically settled within 1–5 business days of registration. Monitor the receivables aging for mortgage-funded sales — delays in bank disbursement create short-term cash flow gaps. In Jordan, banks require the property to be registered in the buyer's name (or the bank's name as mortgagee) before disbursing the mortgage — this ensures the revenue recognition timing and the cash collection timing are closely aligned.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors trace mortgage-funded sale receivables to bank disbursement confirmations. Revenue should not be recognized before registration, even if the bank has verbally committed to the mortgage. Post year-end collections of year-end receivables from mortgage-funded sales provide evidence that the receivable is real and the revenue was appropriately recognized.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Bank mortgage approval letter, sale and purchase agreement, title transfer documentation confirming registration and mortgage annotation, bank disbursement confirmation, accounts receivable aging (mortgage-funded sales), COGS entry for the specific unit, and any conditions precedent to mortgage disbursement.

title: How to Record a Real Estate Sales Broker Commission Paid on Closing a Unit Sale
description: Expensing the agent's commission as a selling cost in the period the sale is completed.
explanation: Agent commissions (typically 2–3% of sale price) are a selling expense in the period the sale is completed. They are not capitalized into the property cost.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Under IFRS 15, incremental costs of obtaining a contract (agent commissions) can be capitalized as a contract cost asset if they are expected to be recovered through the margin on the sale — and expensed only when the unit is handed over and revenue recognized. In practice, many real estate companies expense commissions immediately at sale agreement signing (acceptable as a simplification if the amortization period is less than 12 months). The commission is typically due on signing of the sale agreement or on handover — confirm the contractual trigger.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: The timing of commission expense recognition should match the timing of revenue recognition under IFRS 15. If revenue is deferred to handover but commissions are expensed at contract signing, there is a mismatch — auditors may require the commissions to also be deferred as a contract cost asset. For large development projects with significant sales commissions, this can be material.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Broker agreement specifying the commission rate and trigger event (signing vs. handover), commission invoice, payment confirmation, sales register showing the corresponding unit sale, IFRS 15 contract cost assessment (immediate expense or deferred), and commission accrual at year-end for sales completed but not yet paid.

title: How to Recognize Forfeited Deposit Income When a Property Buyer Cancels Under Contract Terms
description: Releasing the forfeited buyer deposit from deferred revenue to income when a buyer legally cancels their purchase.
explanation: When a buyer legally cancels and forfeits their deposit, the deferred revenue liability is released to income. The developer has fulfilled no obligation but is contractually entitled to keep the funds.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Recognize forfeited deposit income only when the cancellation is confirmed and the developer's right to retain the deposit is legally established (after the contractual notice period and any dispute resolution window). In Jordan, the Real Estate Regulatory Law defines specific rules about refundability depending on the stage of construction and the reason for cancellation — confirm the legal entitlement before recognizing. The unit returns to the available inventory for resale; no COGS is recognized.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the legal basis for forfeiture — the sale and purchase agreement must clearly specify the forfeiture clause and the conditions. Forfeitures made without clear contractual grounds or without appropriate buyer notification expose the developer to legal action and may require the income to be reversed. The forfeiture income should reconcile to the written cancellation notices and legal confirmations received.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sale and purchase agreement (forfeiture clause), buyer cancellation notice, developer's formal response confirming forfeiture, legal counsel confirmation of entitlement, Advance from Buyers sub-ledger release, Forfeited Deposit Income recognition entry, unit reinstatement to inventory, and any disputed cancellations maintained as liability until resolved.

title: How to Refund a Buyer's Deposit When the Developer Is at Fault for a Cancellation
description: Clearing the deferred revenue liability by refunding the buyer's deposit when the developer breaches the contract.
explanation: If the developer fails to deliver on time or breaches the contract, the deposit must be refunded. This simply clears the liability with no income recorded.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: When the developer is at fault (significant delay, material defects, inability to deliver), the full deposit must be refunded. Debit Advance from Buyers (clearing the liability) and credit Cash. No income is recognized. In Jordan, developers who fail to deliver within the contracted timeline are subject to additional penalties under the Real Estate Regulatory Law — these penalties are accounted for separately as a provision under IAS 37 when it becomes probable they will be payable.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test the reasonableness of the developer's characterization of the cancellation — whether the developer is truly at fault (requiring refund) or the buyer (allowing forfeiture). A pattern of refunds at significant financial cost to the developer may indicate construction delays or financial difficulties that have broader going concern implications. Regulatory penalties for late delivery are a separate IAS 37 provision issue.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Cancellation notice and supporting documentation, legal assessment of fault (developer at fault vs. buyer at fault), refund amount calculation, bank transfer confirmation of refund, Advance from Buyers sub-ledger cleared, unit reinstatement to inventory, IAS 37 provision assessment for any additional penalties, and Jordan RERA reporting of the cancellation.

title: How to Record a Post-Handover Instalment Receivable When a Buyer Has a Long-Term Payment Plan
description: Recognizing full revenue at handover while setting up a long-term receivable for the remaining balance payable over multiple years.
explanation: Revenue is recognized at handover regardless of when cash is collected. The outstanding post-handover balance is a long-term receivable. An imputed interest adjustment may be required if the plan is interest-free.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Under IFRS 15, if the payment terms extend significantly beyond one year, a financing component may exist. If the post-handover payment plan is interest-free (or at below-market rates), the receivable must be discounted to present value — the difference between the face value and PV is treated as imputed interest income recognized over the collection period. Assess whether there is a 'significant financing component' using the practical expedient: if the period between performance (handover) and payment is less than one year, no financing adjustment is needed.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test post-handover receivables for the significant financing component. For 3–5 year interest-free payment plans (common in Jordan and GCC off-plan markets), the financing component is material — revenue recognized at handover must be the present value of the receivable, not the face value. IFRS 15 paragraph 62 applies: impute interest if the timing of payments provides the customer with a significant benefit of financing. Aged post-handover receivables also require ECL assessment under IFRS 9.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sale and purchase agreement (post-handover payment schedule, interest rate if any), IFRS 15 significant financing component assessment, discount rate used (market rate for similar financing), PV of post-handover instalments, imputed interest income schedule, IFRS 9 ECL assessment for post-handover receivables, aging of post-handover receivables, and collection history.

title: How to Record the Sale of a Raw Land Plot and Recognize the Gain
description: Removing undeveloped land from inventory or fixed assets and recognizing the gain over its carrying cost.
explanation: Land held for sale is removed from inventory at its cost. The difference between sale price and cost is a gain recognized immediately.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Land is classified as: (a) Inventory (IAS 2) — if held for sale in the ordinary course of business (developer's primary activity); (b) PPE (IAS 16) — if used by the company; or (c) Investment Property (IAS 40) — if held for capital appreciation. The classification affects presentation: land inventory sales are operating revenue; PPE and investment property sales generate gains/losses presented below operating profit. In Jordan, the land gain is subject to income tax — calculate the taxable gain (sale price minus historical cost adjusted for the transfer tax and acquisition costs) and accrue the tax liability.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the cost of land sold against the land register (which should show acquisition cost and all directly attributable costs). Revenue recognition timing: the official title transfer (Lands & Survey Department registration) is the definitive evidence. Land held as development inventory for many years without development activity may need to be reclassified — either as investment property (if held for capital appreciation) or written down to NRV if the market value has declined below cost.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sale and purchase agreement, Lands & Survey Department title transfer certificate, sale proceeds bank receipt, land inventory/fixed asset derecognition at cost, gain calculation, income tax calculation on the gain, Jordan income tax filing, and land register update.

title: How to Recognize Monthly Rental Income from a Commercial Property Tenant
description: Recording one month of earned rental income as the tenant occupies and uses the leased commercial space.
explanation: Rental income is recognized monthly as the right to use the property is provided. This applies whether rent is collected in advance or arrears.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Rental income is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term (if there are rent escalations or rent-free periods — see re-straight-line-lease-incentive). For leases with fixed monthly rent and no escalation, the monthly recognition equals the monthly contracted amount. Set up the lease in the ERP with the start date, end date, monthly rent, and any rent review dates. Generate automatic monthly rent invoices and recognitions. For properties with multiple tenants, maintain a tenant rent roll showing each lease's key terms.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors confirm the tenant is in occupation and the lease is active. Rental income for vacant properties is not recognized — any income accrued for vacant periods is a misstatement. For investment property disclosures, IAS 40 requires disclosure of rental income recognized during the period separately from the fair value gain/loss. Direct operating expenses (repairs, maintenance, insurance) relating to the investment property must also be disclosed.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement (tenant, term, monthly rent, rent review clauses), monthly rent invoice, tenant payment confirmation, rent roll reconciliation (all active leases), vacancy periods tracked separately, IAS 40 investment property income disclosure, and annual straight-line lease income calculation (for leases with escalations).

title: How to Record 12 Months of Advance Rent Received from a Tenant as Unearned Revenue
description: Deferring upfront annual rent as a liability because the obligation to provide occupancy has not yet been fulfilled.
explanation: Common in Jordan where landlords require 12 months in advance. The cash is not revenue yet — it is a liability representing the obligation to provide accommodation each month.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Advance rent received is a liability (Unearned Rental Revenue or Deferred Rental Income) until each month of occupancy is delivered. Set up an amortization schedule releasing 1/12th per month. This is extremely common in Jordan's commercial and residential leasing market where 12-month upfront payments are the norm. For accounting purposes, the substance governs — regardless of the commercial practice, each month's rent is earned only when occupied.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check the Unearned Rental Revenue balance at year-end against the amortization schedule — the balance should equal the remaining months of advance rent × monthly rent. A balance that has not been correctly amortized down overstates the liability and understates revenue. For large commercial leases, auditors may confirm the advance rent amount directly with the tenant.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement specifying the advance rent amount and the lease term, bank receipt for the advance payment, Unearned Rental Revenue amortization schedule (12 months × monthly release), monthly recognition entries, year-end balance confirmation, and tenant confirmation (for material balances).

title: How to Recognize Monthly Rental Income from Previously Collected Advance Rent
description: Moving one month's share of advance rent from the deferred liability to earned rental income.
explanation: Each month, one month's rent is moved from the deferred liability to earned revenue as the tenant occupies and uses the space.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Configure the ERP to automatically release 1/12th of the advance rent balance each month. The Unearned Rental Revenue balance reduces by JOD 5,000 monthly over 12 months until fully earned. At the end of the lease, the Unearned Rental Revenue balance should be zero. When the lease renews and a new advance is received, set up a new 12-month amortization schedule. For mid-year renewals, pro-rate the remaining months correctly.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors reconcile the Unearned Rental Revenue balance at year-end to the remaining months of advance rent in the future periods. They also check that no advance rent relates to leases that have been terminated or are in dispute — in those cases, the deferred balance may need to be refunded or reassessed. Multiple leases with unearned rent should be tracked individually in a sub-ledger.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Unearned Rental Revenue amortization schedule per lease, monthly recognition entry, year-end Unearned Rental Revenue balance reconciliation (advance received minus months earned = remaining balance), lease renewal tracking, and any mid-lease changes (rent review, early termination) requiring schedule adjustment.

title: How to Recognize Rental Income on a Straight-Line Basis for a Lease with Annual Rent Escalations
description: Averaging the total lease revenue over the lease term when a lease includes annual rent increases.
explanation: If a lease has rent escalations, the total lease revenue is averaged and recognized evenly each month. Early months have lower cash receipts but higher P&L revenue, with the difference accrued.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Calculate the straight-line monthly rental income: Total of all contracted monthly rents over the lease term ÷ Number of months. In early lease years (when actual cash is below the straight-line amount), the difference is an Accrued Rental Revenue (asset). In later years (when actual cash exceeds the straight-line amount), the asset is drawn down. For a 5-year lease with rents of JOD 4,000/month in years 1–2 and JOD 5,000/month in years 3–5: straight-line = (24×4,000 + 36×5,000) ÷ 60 = JOD 4,600/month.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors confirm the straight-line income is correctly calculated using the total contracted rents over the full non-cancellable lease term. Rent reviews that are not predetermined (e.g., to market rent at the review date) cannot be straight-lined in advance. The Accrued Rental Revenue asset balance must be assessed for collectability — if the tenant is in financial difficulty, the accrued but not yet billed amount may require impairment.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement with full rent schedule (Year 1–5 rents), straight-line calculation workbook (total rents ÷ months), monthly straight-line income entry, Accrued Rental Revenue schedule (building up in early years, unwinding in later years), ECL assessment on the accrued balance under IFRS 9, and lease term confirmation including any extension options.

title: How to Record a Refundable Tenant Security Deposit Received at Lease Commencement
description: Recording a new tenant's refundable security deposit as a liability rather than rental income.
explanation: Security deposits are not income. They are liabilities because the landlord must return them at the end of the lease if the tenant has not caused damage.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Tenant security deposits are financial liabilities — they must be returned at lease end (less any deductions for damage). Maintain a Tenant Deposits Payable sub-ledger per tenant showing the deposit amount, receipt date, and any deductions made. Segregate deposit funds from operating cash in a dedicated deposit account (best practice and in some jurisdictions legally required). Under IFRS 9, assess whether the deposit should be discounted to present value if it is expected to be held for more than 12 months and the discount is material.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors confirm that security deposits are not being recognized as income. A sub-ledger of all outstanding deposits should match the Tenant Deposits Payable balance. Deposits for tenants who have vacated but not yet received a refund are the highest-risk items — auditors will investigate whether the delay is a dispute over deductions or simply an administrative delay. IFRS 9 discounting assessment: for long-term deposits, the time value of money may be material.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement specifying the deposit amount and refund conditions, deposit receipt confirmation, Tenant Deposits Payable sub-ledger per tenant, dedicated deposit bank account (if applicable), end-of-lease inspection report and deduction schedule, IFRS 9 discounting assessment for long-term deposits, and any jurisdiction-specific deposit protection scheme compliance.

title: How to Record the Return of a Tenant Security Deposit at Lease End After a Clean Inspection
description: Clearing the security deposit liability by refunding the full amount when no deductions are required.
explanation: This clears the deposit liability once the property has been inspected and no deductions are required.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Process the refund only after the property inspection confirms no damage and the tenant's account is clear (no outstanding rent arrears). Debit Tenant Deposits Payable and credit Cash — the Tenant Deposits Payable sub-ledger for this tenant goes to zero. Send a formal refund confirmation letter to the tenant. If any interest was earned on the deposit during the lease (where legally required to hold deposits in interest-bearing accounts), pay the interest proportional to the tenant's deposit.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test that refunds are only made after inspection — refunds without inspection records suggest inadequate internal controls. Old Tenant Deposits Payable balances for tenants who vacated many months ago without a refund or deduction decision are a concern — they suggest either outstanding disputes or administrative failures. Any interest earned on deposit funds that should be returned to the tenant but is instead retained by the landlord is a compliance issue.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: End-of-lease property inspection report (no damages noted), tenant's clear rent account confirmation, refund authorization, bank transfer confirmation, Tenant Deposits Payable sub-ledger cleared to zero, tenant refund confirmation letter, and any interest calculation (if applicable).

title: How to Record a Partial Tenant Deposit Forfeiture to Cover Property Damage Costs
description: Retaining part of a tenant's security deposit for damage repairs, refunding the balance, and recognizing the forfeited amount as income.
explanation: If a tenant causes damage, the cost is recovered from the deposit. The retained portion is recognized as Other Income since the obligation to refund is extinguished.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The forfeited deposit portion (JOD 3,000 for damage) represents compensation for repairs — recognize as Other Income when the deduction decision is confirmed and documented. The actual repair costs, when incurred, are expensed separately as maintenance/repairs expense. The net P&L impact: Other Income from forfeiture offset by the Repairs Expense for fixing the damage. If the deposit is insufficient to cover the damage, the shortfall is a recovery from the tenant — create a receivable and assess collectability under IFRS 9.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors require objective evidence of damage to justify the deposit deduction — photographs, inspection reports, contractor repair quotes, and invoices. Arbitrary deductions without documentation expose the landlord to legal action. The repair cost incurred must be compared to the deposit retained — if the repair cost is less than the deduction, the excess over repair cost may not qualify as income.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: End-of-lease property inspection report with damage photographs, damage assessment report, repair quotation and invoice (for actual costs), deposit deduction notice to tenant, partial refund bank transfer, Other Income recognition for the forfeited amount, Repairs and Maintenance expense for actual costs, shortfall receivable assessment (if damage exceeds deposit), and any tenant dispute correspondence.

title: How to Charge and Record a Late Rent Payment Penalty from a Tenant
description: Recognizing a penalty fee as Other Income when a tenant pays rent after the contractual due date.
explanation: Late payment penalties are recognized as Other Income when charged to the tenant. They compensate the landlord for the time value of money lost from delayed receipts.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Configure the ERP to auto-calculate late payment penalties based on the lease terms — typically a fixed daily or monthly charge, or a percentage of the overdue amount, from the day after the due date. Generate the penalty invoice automatically when rent remains unpaid beyond the grace period. Tag penalty income to a separate Other Income account (not rental income) for management reporting clarity. In Jordan, lease agreements must clearly specify the penalty mechanism — penalties without contractual basis are unenforceable.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check that late payment penalties are only charged when the lease agreement specifically entitles the landlord to do so and when the rent was genuinely overdue. Penalties charged on disputed rent amounts (where the tenant is withholding for a legitimate reason) may need to be provisioned against. A systematic pattern of late payment may also indicate a tenant under financial stress — flag for ECL assessment under IFRS 9.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement (late payment penalty clause, grace period, rate), rent due date evidence, penalty calculation, penalty invoice issued to tenant, tenant acknowledgment or payment, and IFRS 9 ECL assessment for tenants with persistent late payment patterns.

title: How to Bill a Commercial Tenant for Their Share of Common Area Maintenance Costs
description: Invoicing a tenant for their proportional share of building operating costs under a triple-net or service charge lease.
explanation: Many commercial leases are 'triple net' — tenants pay their proportional share of building operating costs. This is recognized as revenue when billed.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Maintain a service charge account showing all recoverable building operating costs (utilities, cleaning, security, insurance, maintenance) and each tenant's proportional share based on their leased floor area as a percentage of total leasable area. Bill quarterly or annually depending on the lease terms. For estimated service charges, set up a reconciliation at year-end comparing actual costs to estimated charges — rebate excesses or raise deficiency invoices. Present service charge revenue separately from base rental revenue on the income statement.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that service charge calculations are consistent with the lease terms (both the recoverable cost categories and the allocation method). Under IFRS 15, assess whether the landlord is acting as principal (recognizes gross service charge and gross costs) or agent (recognizes only the management margin) — this depends on whether the landlord has control over the services before providing them to the tenant.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Lease agreement (service charge provisions, recoverable cost categories, allocation method), service charge budget, actual cost schedule, tenant proportional share calculation, service charge invoice, year-end reconciliation (actual vs. estimated), and IFRS 15 principal vs. agent assessment.

title: How to Reverse Accrued Rental Income When a Unit Becomes Vacant Mid-Month
description: Removing previously recognized rental income for the period after a tenant vacates unexpectedly.
explanation: If a tenant vacates earlier than expected and rent cannot be collected for that period, any previously accrued income must be reversed to avoid overstating revenue.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Reverse the accrual in the period the vacancy is confirmed — when the tenant physically vacates and it is clear rent will not be collected for the remaining period. For tenants who vacate before their lease expiry, assess whether the remaining lease obligations create a recoverable receivable (if the tenant is in breach) or must be reversed (if the landlord waives the obligation). Update the occupancy schedule and vacancy tracker in the property management system.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check that accrued rental revenue is reversed promptly when vacancy occurs rather than being left on the balance sheet as an uncollectible asset. An aged Accrued Rental Revenue balance for vacant units is a misstatement. They also review whether the vacancy is covered by a rental guarantee (from a developer or guarantor) — if so, the guarantee claim replaces the tenant receivable.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Tenant vacancy notification or vacate date evidence, reversal journal entry dated to the vacancy date, updated occupancy schedule, rental guarantee assessment (if applicable), ECL assessment for any remaining tenant receivables, and property management system vacancy update.

title: How to Recognize Monthly Property Management Fee Revenue
description: Recording the monthly management commission earned for managing a property on behalf of an owner.
explanation: Management fees (typically 5–10% of collected rent) are recognized as revenue in the month the management service is provided.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Property management fee revenue is recognized monthly as the management service is delivered — this is a service over time under IFRS 15. The fee is typically a percentage of rent collected (variable consideration) or a fixed monthly fee. For percentage-based fees, recognize only when the underlying rent is collected (the trigger for the variable consideration). Deduct the management fee from the gross rent collected before remitting to the owner (see re-mgmt-owner-distribution-payout).
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors confirm the fee rate against the management agreement. Under IFRS 15, the management company is an agent — it recognizes only the net fee, not gross rent collected. Fees recognized on rent that was not collected (accrued but unpaid by the tenant) require an ECL assessment. If the management company also charges the owner for maintenance recharges and other services, each performance obligation is assessed separately.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Property management agreement (fee rate, performance obligations, payment terms), monthly management fee calculation (% × collected rent or fixed fee), fee invoice to owner, owner payment confirmation, per-property management fee ledger, and IFRS 15 performance obligation assessment.

title: How to Record a Maintenance Cost Paid by the Manager and Recharged to the Property Owner
description: Passing through a third-party repair cost to the owner with no net margin for the property manager.
explanation: The manager pays the contractor, records the expense, and immediately bills the owner. The net effect is zero income — the manager is a pass-through agent for this cost.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: This pass-through recording is used when the property manager acts as principal (pays the contractor and is responsible for the work quality) — present gross expense and gross recovery revenue. If the manager acts purely as an agent (the owner contracts directly with the contractor and the manager only facilitates), record only the fee earned for arranging the work. Maintain owner approval records for all maintenance work above a pre-approved threshold — unauthorized recharges create disputes and potential bad debt exposure.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors test the principal vs. agent classification for maintenance recharges under IFRS 15. If the manager always passes costs at zero margin with no risk, it may be acting as agent — presenting net (just the fee) may be more appropriate. For the principal presentation, verify that actual contractor invoices support the recharge and that no markup has been applied (unless the management agreement permits a markup).
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Owner authorization for the maintenance work (above threshold), contractor invoice, payment to contractor, recharge invoice to owner, management agreement confirming recharge terms and any markup entitlement, and IFRS 15 principal vs. agent assessment.

title: How to Record the Net Rental Distribution Payment to a Property Owner
description: Remitting the net rental proceeds to the property owner after deducting management fees and approved expenses.
explanation: This clears the liability to the owner created when rent was collected. The distribution is net of the management fee and any approved expenses.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The monthly owner distribution clears the Due to Landlord liability. The distribution amount = Gross rent collected − Management fee − Approved maintenance recharges − Other authorized deductions. Provide the owner with a detailed monthly statement showing: rent collected, management fee, approved expenses, and net distribution. Remit by the agreed date in the management agreement — late remittances create liability and potential contractual penalties.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors reconcile the Due to Landlord balance to the sum of rent collected minus fees and expenses minus distributions made. An unexplained balance indicates either un-remitted funds (cash flow problem) or unrecorded deductions. The property manager must not use owner funds for its own operations — commingling client funds with operating cash is a regulatory compliance breach.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Monthly owner statement (rent collected, deductions, net distribution), bank transfer confirmation, Due to Landlord sub-ledger cleared per owner, management agreement remittance terms, owner fund bank account statement (segregated), and any disputed deductions log.

title: How to Create a Vacancy Loss Provision for Expected Empty Units in a Managed Portfolio
description: Estimating and recording the expected income loss from vacant units in a property portfolio at year-end.
explanation: For larger managed portfolios, a provision for vacancy is created at year-end to reflect the economic reality that not all units will be occupied 100% of the time.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: A vacancy loss provision is appropriate for portfolios where historical vacancy rates are measurable and recurring. Calculate using historical occupancy data: typical vacancy rate × annual rental income × remaining months in the year. This provision is more common in property fund accounting than in individual asset accounting. Review and update the provision at each reporting date based on the current occupancy schedule and forward lease commitments.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors assess whether the vacancy provision meets the IAS 37 criteria: present obligation, probable outflow, reliable estimate. A provision for future vacancies (where no specific unit is identified as vacant) may not qualify as an IAS 37 provision — it may instead be presented as management commentary on market conditions. The provision should be reversed when the vacant unit is re-let.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Portfolio occupancy schedule, historical vacancy rate data (minimum 2 years), provision calculation methodology, current vacant units identified, forward lease commitments, IAS 37 three-part test assessment, and provision roll-forward.

title: How to Expense Routine Building Maintenance Costs Including Painting and Minor Repairs
description: Recording routine maintenance that preserves the building in its current condition as a period expense.
explanation: Routine maintenance that preserves the building in its current condition is expensed immediately. Only improvements that extend the asset's life are capitalized.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: The capital vs. expense decision is the most important judgment in building maintenance accounting. The test under IAS 16: does the expenditure restore the asset to its original condition (expense) or enhance it beyond its original condition or extend its life (capitalize)? Painting walls to maintain appearance = expense. Upgrading to energy-efficient LED lighting throughout = potentially capitalizable. Implement a capitalization threshold (e.g., JOD 5,000 per single work item) below which all maintenance is expensed.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors review large maintenance invoices to test the capitalize vs. expense decision. A large maintenance program (e.g., full building refurbishment) broken into multiple smaller invoices to avoid the capitalization threshold is a misstatement (substance over form). Conversely, capitalizing routine repainting or decorating overstates assets and understates maintenance expense.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Maintenance contractor invoice with scope of work description, capital vs. expense assessment (IAS 16 test), maintenance log, approval for maintenance work (owner or building manager authorization), and capitalization threshold policy document.

title: How to Record and Amortize an Annual Facilities Management Contract as a Prepaid Asset
description: Paying an FM company annually to manage technical systems and maintenance, amortized monthly over the service period.
explanation: An annual FM contract is a prepaid asset. JOD 3,000 moves to FM Expense each month to match the cost to the period the service is provided.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Set up a 12-month amortization schedule releasing JOD 3,000 per month. The FM contract typically covers: planned preventive maintenance (PPM), corrective maintenance response, and technical system management (HVAC, fire systems, electrical). Evaluate whether the FM contract qualifies as a lease under IFRS 16 — if the contract grants the right to use a specific identified asset (e.g., a dedicated maintenance vehicle) for a period, IFRS 16 recognition may be required for that element.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors confirm the contract period against the prepaid amortization schedule. If the FM company has underperformed (e.g., systemic failures to respond to maintenance requests), assess whether the full prepaid amount is recoverable — an impairment or advance payment dispute may be appropriate. For buildings with multiple FM contracts (elevator, HVAC, fire, cleaning), ensure all are tracked and amortized correctly.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: FM contract (scope, term, annual fee), payment confirmation, prepaid amortization schedule, monthly FM Expense release entries, IFRS 16 embedded lease assessment, FM company performance records, and contract renewal tracking.

title: How to Record and Amortize an Annual Elevator Maintenance and Certification Contract
description: Capitalizing the annual elevator service contract fee as a prepaid asset and releasing it monthly.
explanation: Elevator service contracts are mandatory in most jurisdictions for multi-floor buildings. The annual fee is prepaid and amortized at JOD 400/month.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Elevator maintenance is a mandatory regulatory requirement in Jordan — buildings must hold a current elevator certification. Set up the 12-month prepaid amortization (JOD 4,800 ÷ 12 = JOD 400/month). Track the certification renewal date — operating an elevator without a valid certificate creates both a regulatory liability and a significant personal injury liability. If the elevator requires a major overhaul or replacement, that cost is capitalized as a separate component under IAS 16 component accounting.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the elevator certification is current at the reporting date. Buildings with expired elevator certifications may require a liability provision for regulatory fines. Any major elevator repair or replacement that extends useful life must be assessed for capitalization rather than expensing through the prepaid maintenance structure.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Elevator service contract (scope, term, annual fee), payment confirmation, elevator certification certificate (current validity), monthly amortization schedule, elevator inspection report, and any major repair or replacement invoices (capitalization assessment).

title: How to Record Common Area Utility Costs for Lobbies, Parking, and Corridors in a Multi-Tenant Building
description: Expensing electricity and water costs for shared building areas that may be recovered through tenant service charges.
explanation: Common area utilities are an operating cost of the building. In a triple-net lease arrangement, these are typically recharged to tenants through the service charge mechanism.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Track common area utilities separately from tenant-specific utility costs. Where submetering exists, charge each tenant directly for their own consumption; the common area element is pooled and allocated pro-rata by floor area. Accrue utilities monthly if bills arrive after period-close. For buildings with significant common area costs, benchmark the cost per sqm against industry norms — excessive utility costs may indicate technical issues (HVAC inefficiency, water leaks) requiring investigation.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors check that common area utility costs are correctly categorized — costs that are directly metered to specific tenants (and recovered from them) are not common area costs. For investment property disclosure under IAS 40, direct operating expenses (including utilities) must be disclosed separately for properties that generated rental income vs. those that did not.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Utility invoices (electricity, water, common areas), meter readings confirming common area vs. tenant allocation, service charge recovery calculation, monthly accrual entries, utility cost per sqm analysis, and IAS 40 operating expense disclosure.

title: How to Record and Amortize an Annual Property and Liability Insurance Premium
description: Paying the yearly building structure and public liability insurance premium, amortized monthly over the coverage year.
explanation: Building insurance is a prepaid asset, expensed at JOD 1,000 per month over the 12-month coverage period.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Property insurance typically covers: building structure (replacement cost basis), public/third-party liability, loss of rent (business interruption), and sometimes tenant contents (where landlord responsibility). Set up a 12-month amortization at JOD 1,000/month. Ensure the sum insured reflects the current replacement value of the building — under-insurance triggers the average clause, proportionally reducing any claim recovery. Review coverage annually when the policy renews.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify the policy is current (not lapsed) at the reporting date. The sum insured must be compared to the building's current reinstatement value — if the carrying value significantly exceeds the sum insured, the company may be under-insured (a contingent liability). Any insurance claims in progress must be assessed for the recognition of an insurance receivable (when virtually certain of recovery).
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Insurance policy schedule (coverage type, sum insured, premium, renewal date), payment confirmation, prepaid amortization schedule, reinstatement value assessment, any active claims documentation, and sum insured vs. reinstatement value comparison.

title: How to Record Monthly Building Security Guard Service Costs
description: Expensing the monthly cost of a contracted security company as a recurring building operating cost.
explanation: Security is a recurring operating cost expensed monthly as the service is rendered.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Security service costs are expensed monthly as the service is provided. For multi-tenant buildings, include security costs in the service charge reconciliation — they are typically a recoverable common area operating cost. Assess the security contract for an IFRS 16 embedded lease — if the security company provides dedicated vehicles assigned specifically to the building, those may constitute a lease element requiring separate recognition.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors verify that the security service is genuine and that staff on the security contract are genuinely independent contractors (not de facto employees of the building owner). For security costs recharged to tenants, confirm the amount recharged is consistent with the service charge provisions in the lease. Security overpayments or invoices for services not received are a fraud risk.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Security service agreement (scope, monthly fee, personnel commitment), monthly invoice, payment confirmation, security guard deployment log, service charge recovery calculation, and IFRS 16 embedded lease assessment.

title: How to Record Monthly Landscaping and Common Area Cleaning Service Costs
description: Expensing the monthly cost of maintaining gardens and common area cleanliness as building operating expenses.
explanation: Ongoing cleaning and landscaping are necessary to maintain the property's appeal and value. They are period expenses, not capital improvements.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Landscaping and cleaning are recurring operating costs that preserve the property's condition and appeal. Include in the service charge recovery calculation for commercial buildings. For investment properties, these costs reduce net operating income (NOI) — the key metric used for fair value assessment under the income capitalization approach. Track cost per sqm of maintained area as an operational efficiency metric.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors distinguish between routine landscaping/cleaning (expense) and significant landscape redesign or major renovation of common areas (potentially capitalizable). A complete redesign of the building's landscaping that enhances the property's value may qualify for capitalization under IAS 16 component accounting. The IAS 40 investment property note requires disclosure of direct operating expenses for properties that generated rental income.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Service agreement (scope, monthly fee), monthly invoice, service delivery confirmation (work records or supervisor sign-off), service charge recovery allocation, annual landscaping vs. capital improvement assessment, and IAS 40 operating expense disclosure.

title: How to Record a Monthly Sinking Fund Contribution for Future Major Building Repairs
description: Setting aside restricted cash each month in a sinking fund designated for future capital expenditure.
explanation: Sinking fund contributions are restricted cash set aside for future capital expenditure (roof replacement, façade renovation). They remain an asset until spent.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: Present the sinking fund as a restricted asset (current or non-current depending on the planned spending horizon) — separate from operating cash. Under owners association accounting, each unit owner's contribution accumulates in a pooled sinking fund account. The sinking fund is a balance sheet asset — contributions are not expenses when made (the expense is recognized when the fund is used for maintenance or repairs). Interest earned on the sinking fund balance is credited to the fund.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors confirm the sinking fund is genuinely segregated in a separate bank account and has not been commingled with operating cash. They also check whether the accumulated sinking fund balance is sufficient for the planned expenditure — an under-funded sinking fund may require a catch-up contribution. The restricted nature of the fund must be disclosed in the financial statements.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sinking fund policy (contribution rate, purpose, management), sinking fund bank account statement, monthly contribution records, restriction disclosure, interest earned on the fund, planned capital expenditure schedule, and adequacy assessment (current balance vs. planned spend).

title: How to Use Sinking Fund Cash for a Major Building Repair or Capital Improvement
description: Drawing on the sinking fund to pay for a major repair, with the cost capitalized or expensed based on its nature.
explanation: When the repair qualifies as a capital improvement it is debited to the asset; if it is merely maintenance it is debited to expense. Either way, the sinking fund is drawn down.

practitioner_notes.erp_application: When the sinking fund is used: (a) debit the fixed asset (Building) if the expenditure enhances the asset or extends its useful life — this is a capital improvement; or (b) debit Maintenance Expense if it merely maintains the status quo. The sinking fund (Restricted Asset) is credited in both cases. The restricted nature of the sinking fund is released on spending — the asset transfers from restricted to the fixed asset or expense account.
practitioner_notes.audit_triggers: Auditors apply the same capital vs. expense test as for general building maintenance (see re-building-maintenance-expense). The source of funding (sinking fund vs. operating cash) does not change the accounting treatment — a maintenance expense is still a maintenance expense even if paid from the sinking fund. They also confirm the sinking fund balance after the draw-down matches the bank account.
practitioner_notes.required_documentation: Sinking fund withdrawal authorization, contractor invoice for the work done, scope of work description, capital vs. expense assessment, fixed asset register update (if capitalized), sinking fund balance before and after the draw-down, building repair completion confirmation, and updated useful life assessment for the component replaced.

title: How to Record a Construction Mortgage Tranche Drawdown from the Bank
